Instead you found the programme wrote a new criterion onto the sheet, "Founder command of the business," scored from office-hours contact, and Olivia Ward gave her highest command scores to founders she already had context on, the ones introduced through someone, while Daniel Kim's log gives open-call founders 13 minutes against 21 for introduced.
brief.context:
Coldharbour Launch is a twelve-week pre-seed programme run by the enterprise centre of a university in a northern English city. The spring 2026 cohort is eighteen ventures, about forty volunteer mentors, and a programme team of three. It ends in Selection Day, where a mentor panel scores every venture on a sheet and three ventures take a 25,000 pound follow-on grant and introductions to an angel syndicate.

In January the board licensed Pitchwright, an AI writing copilot, and required every founder to write their weekly one-page update and their Selection Day deck in it. The board paper's aim was to level the field between founders who arrive with business vocabulary and first-time founders, so that Selection Day would judge the venture and not the founder's writing.

What made me want to study it is that the aim and the mentors' behaviour pulled apart within about three weeks, and I was in the room while it happened. The updates converged in structure and phrasing, mentors stopped reading them, and judgment moved onto the office-hours slot. In week seven the programme wrote that move onto the scoring sheet as a fifth line, "Founder command of the business", scored from office-hours contact rather than from the deck. This is a live case of an AI tool changing what expert evaluators attend to, with the evaluators giving their own account of the shift while it is happening.

Three features make the setting unusually tractable. The aim was written down in a board paper before the tool arrived. Use was required of all eighteen ventures, so heavy or light use is not a self-selected confound. And the same scoring sheet was used on a previous cohort without the tool.

Two things to be honest about. I did not select this site from a population of programmes; I was already its critical friend when the licensing decision landed, so this is a convenience sample. And the mentors know who I am and what I am watching for, so some of what I hear about fairness may be performed at me, and I have no clean way to rule that out.
brief.siteRationale:
Why this is the right place. Four things, and they are unusual together. The programme wrote its aim down before the tool arrived, in a January board paper, so there is a stated intention to hold the outcome against rather than one reconstructed afterwards. Use of Pitchwright was required of all eighteen ventures, so heavy or light use is not a choice that confounds the comparison. Every venture is scored on a sheet at one fixed moment, Selection Day, so the judgment is recorded rather than inferred. And a previous cohort was scored on the same sheet without the tool. On top of that the mentors narrate the shift themselves, in office hours, in interviews and in their own Slack channel, while it is happening.

What the place is bad at showing me. Coldharbour Launch is one programme in one city running one tool with one cohort, and its Selection Day scores are produced by a panel that deliberates in private. So the site can show that mentors' attention moved from the page to the room and who gained by that, but it cannot show that the tool caused the move rather than merely accompanied it, and it cannot show any individual mentor's reasoning apart from the joint score.

Upstream of that, I cannot see what Pitchwright did inside anyone's writing process. I have the outputs, the one-pagers and the decks, and the usage log telling me which ventures used it heavily and which barely. I do not have drafts, prompts, or what a founder pasted in against what the tool handed back. So when Hannah Foster says the first page made her sound like she knew what she was doing, I am taking her word for the mechanism.

Two further limits I should state rather than manage. The mentors know I am the programme's critical friend, so some of the fairness talk may be performed at me. And convergence in the pages could come from founders copying each other rather than from the tool. The checks available to me there are all output-side: this cohort's pages against the previous cohort's, heavy users against light users from the usage log, and phrase-level repetition such as the three ventures Olivia Ward saw using "underserved by incumbents" in the same week.

What I can defend is that set of within-programme comparisons plus the evaluators' own accounts. What I cannot offer is a counterfactual programme. A reviewer who wants causal identification should not be reading this paper.
brief.processOfInterest:
The process I am studying is the in-room evaluation: a mentor probing a founder off script in the weekly office-hours slot and updating a judgment. One instance is a single slot, from the opening through the unscripted probe and the interruptions to the word the mentor writes next to the name afterwards. It repeats weekly, roughly ten times per venture across the cohort. Leah Morgan's week-4 slot is a clean instance: the rehearsed Pitchwright deck delivered as a monologue, Ravi saying "right, now forget all that, what did the restaurant say when you turned up", the freeze, the kitchen porter story, and "there's something there" written next to her name.

It has an origin and a place it lands, and I was sloppy for a while about not separating those from the thing itself.

The origin is the mentor attention shift: each mentor reads the weekly written update until it stops giving them anything, then stops reading it, permanently. That is short and one-way, over in two or three weeks. Ravi stopped in week two, Olivia around week three. I cannot put a page count on the threshold; both say they read a handful of interchangeable pages and quit. That is a rate in the loose sense, not a measured dose, and there is no log of mentor reading that would make it one. So I define that instance as first read to stated stopping point, and treat the page count as something I noticed rather than something I measured.

Where it lands is the venture's evaluation across the full twelve weeks: one instance is a single venture, running from its first office-hours slot through the weekly update and the mid-cohort sheet to Selection Day scoring. Eighteen of those run in parallel in this cohort.

So three linked processes: an origin that runs on each mentor's own exposure and finishes early, a repeated in-room evaluation that is the one I am tracking, and a twelve-week accumulation that carries the outcome.
brief.outcomeOfInterest:
The outcome is which ventures are selected, and on what grounds mentors say they judged. For the study to be worth doing I need to see differences in four places.

Across cohorts, in how far selection tracks prior introduction. Last cohort one of three grants went to an introduced founder. This cohort three of three: Kerbside, Bramble and Fenwick Labs. Same programme, same grant, same sheet for four of its five lines.

Within this cohort, between introduced and open-call founders: slot length, where Daniel Kim's log gives 21 minutes against 13, interruption counts, and the command score.

Within this cohort, between heavy and light users of the tool from the usage log, in how far their pages converged. That is the check that separates the tool from the programme's template or from founders copying each other.

Between what mentors say they score and what they say they actually do: the sheet against the room and the Slack channel, where Ethan Brooks writes that the pages are all fine and he cannot rank fine against fine.

The single result a reviewer should sit up at is Loomly and Tallow, both open call, highest on traction and lowest on command.

The confound I have to handle. Two things changed between the cohorts, not one: the tool arrived in week one and the fifth line in week seven. What I can show is the ordering, and it is documented rather than reconstructed. Chloe's memo says under "What we have heard" that mentors report the updates are uniform and that they are reading less into them, and that two no longer read them before office hours. The sheet change is downstream of the abandonment by the programme's own account, so the line did not appear for unrelated reasons.

What that does not close is whether the fifth line carries the whole difference. The test is to rescore this cohort on the four lines the previous cohort also had. I am recording my expectation before running it: I expect the introduced founders would not still be on top, or only narrowly, because Loomly and Tallow are strongest on traction, which is one of the four shared lines.

If that is what it shows, the claim shrinks and I will let it shrink. It becomes: a required writing tool emptied the artefact of information, the programme responded by scoring the interaction instead, and the criterion it added is the one that tracks prior acquaintance. That puts the causal weight on the programme's response rather than on the tool, which is not what I set out expecting. Two cohorts on each side would settle it and I do not have them.
brief.bind:
Three binds, nested, and the one that should anchor the paper is the founders'.

The founders are caught between complying with a required tool that makes them sound like everyone else, and going off-script to be seen, which risks reading as unprepared. Hannah Foster resolves it by doing both and paying twice: the Pitchwright page for the programme, because Daniel checks it has been submitted, and a second page she writes by hand, two ugly columns of numbers and what people actually said, for the room. That is the bind with an artefact attached. Her own account of the cost is exact: the tool took away the one thing she could get good at on her own, at home, at night, and moved the whole thing into a room where the people who are already comfortable win. Leah Morgan is the same bind without the workaround, which is why her week-4 slot comes out as a rehearsed monologue.

What makes it a bind rather than a grievance is that she has nowhere to put it. The weekly update is the channel, and the channel is what she is complaining about. Office hours are fifteen minutes and she spends them being interrupted about parent pricing. The sheet has no line for it. She said it to me in a cafe in week eight and nowhere else. And her actual ask is one the programme cannot grant on its own terms: read the pages, or stop pretending the pages are the point, either, not both. Granting the second half concedes the board paper was wrong inside a term.

The mentors are caught between the fairness aim they were given and their sense that the page no longer tells them anything, so they fall back on the room and on who they know. Olivia Ward is the clearest case: she says the room felt more real, then that she gives her highest command scores to founders she already had context on, then that she went back to the thing the page was supposed to stop her relying on, and when I asked whether it was fairer she said honestly, no. Ravi Patel holds both halves in one sentence: not blaming the tool, and then we rank on something else, and the something else is worse.

Chloe Park is caught between the board's promise and a result that looks worse on the promise's own terms. Her bind is visible in what one sentence becomes between two audiences. On Slack in week five, to the mentors, she proposes the new line so we are at least scoring the room openly rather than pretending we score the deck. In the week-7 memo, to everyone, the same fact reads: this makes explicit what mentors say they are already doing. The pretence is edited out and the fairness aim is left standing, and the board paper is never retracted. So the contradiction is named once, informally, and then absorbed into procedure. That act is what turned a mentor habit into a scored criterion.

Who feels the pull hardest: the open-call founders, Hannah and Leah, and after them the mentors who have noticed what they are doing, Olivia and Ravi. Gabriel Martinez is the one person whose expectation and outcome still match, and he is not caught at all, which is itself a finding.
brief.sampleRationale:
The sample has to vary on three things for the comparisons to hold: route into the programme (introduced through a mentor against the open call), prior business vocabulary (corporate, MBA or family business against a first venture), and Pitchwright use (heavy against light, from the usage log). The previous cohort supplies the fourth line of variation, the same sheet without the tool.

There are two units. The venture is the unit for anything countable, and there the variation is already present because it is a census rather than a sample: all eighteen ventures' weekly updates, their usage figures, and their Selection Day sheets, plus the previous cohort's sheets on the four shared lines. Roughly a third of the eighteen came in introduced, two thirds through the open call. The office-hours slot is the second unit and the one where the judgment is actually formed, and that is a sample: about thirty slots across four mentors over ten weeks. Seven founder interviews were chosen to fill cells, Hannah Foster and Leah Morgan open call, Gabriel Martinez, Samuel Price and Natalie Hayes introduced, crossed with heavy and light use.

Three weaknesses I have to state rather than manage. First, the slot sample is mentor-weighted: Ravi Patel's Thursday office hours carries close to half of it, so the attention shift I can document as observation is his. Olivia Ward's I have from her week-six interview and Ethan Brooks's only from the Slack channel. In the observed slots the introduced and heavy-use founders are mostly Ravi's founders, so mentor and cell are not separable yet. Second, Olivia's slots skew open-call and Ethan's are the short ones, so simply watching them more adds coverage without rebalancing the cells. Third, introduced plus light user may not exist as a lived combination in this cohort, which would mean route in and usage are confounded in who the founders are, not merely in who I watched, and neither comparison could then stand alone.

Two things I can settle without new fieldwork, and will before I write this section: cross-tabulate the observed slots by mentor, route in and usage from the fieldnotes, which name the founder and start time for every slot, and check the usage log for whether the introduced/light cell exists across all eighteen. Crossed both ways at interview level the cells stay one or two deep, and I will report them that way.

What has to be run before this goes to a journal, not planned. The check is right that an AMJ reviewer will not accept a causal story about the programme's response resting on two interviewed founders and one aggregate contrast. Three things move from intention to completed work before submission, and all three run on material already in my drive. First, tabulate the command line and the four shared lines for all eighteen ventures in this cohort, so the traction-against-command inversion is a distribution rather than Loomly and Tallow. Second, run the rescore on the old four lines and report it against the pre-registered expectation I wrote at Outcome, which is that the introduced founders would not still be on top. Third, recode the ten weeks of fieldnotes for artefact refusals and floor-taking per slot against a written definition, which turns the stopping-rate claim from something I noticed into something I measured. Until the third is done the stopping rate stays labelled as noticed and not measured, and the claim it supports is stated as two mentors' timing and reasons corroborated across interview, Slack and memo, not as a cohort-level rate.
brief.earlySurprise:
Four things the material has shown me that I did not go in expecting.

Mentors stopped reading the page rather than reading it differently. I expected polished, comparable updates to be judged more alike. Instead Olivia Ward stopped at about week three because everybody's pages were decent and that was the problem, Ravi Patel stopped in week two after three updates that were the same page with the company name changed, and Ethan Brooks kept reading and found he could not rank fine against fine. A tool brought in to make the artefact comparable made it uninformative.

The programme then wrote the room onto the sheet. Chloe Park's week-7 memo adds "Founder command of the business", scored from office-hours contact rather than the deck, and says in terms that this makes explicit what mentors are already doing. Within seven weeks the organisation formalised the thing the intervention was meant to remove, in writing, and said so.

The founders with the best evidence were the ones the new criterion punished. Loomly and Tallow scored highest on traction and lowest on command. I had assumed command and substance would at least point the same way.

The advantaged founder is not unaware of his advantage. I expected Gabriel Martinez to tell a merit story. He does not: he says the page was never the field, that the tool has cleared the page out of the way so the room is all that is left, which suits him, and that it is not the deck, it is the door. He also thinks the room is the right test. That is a competing theory of what should count as evidence, held by the person it favours, and it is not obviously wrong.

What cuts against the pattern, and what I have not checked. The one moment the room opened for an open-call founder is Leah Morgan's week-4 slot: she delivered the Pitchwright deck as a monologue, Ravi told her to forget it and asked what the restaurant actually said, and she gave him the kitchen porter. That is the only point in that fieldnote where he leans forward, and he wrote "there's something there" rather than the "fine" Hannah got. Her command score still came out low. On the other side I have not read the command line for the fifteen ventures I did not interview, so I cannot yet rule out an introduced founder scoring badly on command, or an open-call founder scoring well simply because they are comfortable being interrupted. Gabriel's account predicts the latter should exist. Until I tabulate all eighteen I am arguing from two founders and an aggregate, and I will say so rather than round it up.

One more thing the material shows that I had stopped seeing. The last paragraph of my own week-4 fieldnote is a note to self: count interruptions per slot next week, check who came in through an introduction, the open-call founders are getting the shorter slots. That dates my noticing of the slot-length gap to week 4, in the room, three weeks before Daniel Kim's log gave me 21 minutes against 13 to put under it. It also records a measurement I promised myself and never made. I have three counts from that one afternoon and no more: Hannah four interruptions in eleven minutes, Gabriel one in twenty-four, Leah none until Ravi stopped her outright. I dropped the tally because I could not settle what counts, and I will not pretend otherwise. Recoding is possible from material I already hold, and it needs two counts per slot rather than one: artefact refusals at the opening, where a mentor puts the page aside before the founder has used it, and floor-taking during the answer. Those are different acts, and only the first is the behaviour this study is about.
brief.startingInterest:
A university pre-seed programme required every founder to write their weekly one-page update and their Selection Day deck in an AI writing copilot, Pitchwright, so that Selection Day would judge the venture and not the founder's writing. Within about three weeks that aim and what the mentors actually did pulled apart. Ravi Patel stopped reading the updates in week one because they were the same page with the company name changed, and ran office hours with the laptop closed instead: a printed list of eighteen venture names, one word beside each after the slot. His own gloss was that the tool made the pages identical, so all he has left is the room, and the room is who is comfortable being interrupted.

The programme then wrote the room onto the sheet. Chloe Park's week-7 memo adds a fifth Selection Day line, "Founder command of the business", weighted equally with team, market, traction and plan and scored from office-hours contact rather than the deck. Ravi, after she left: they have put the room on the sheet.

What I want to study is that sequence and who it favours. Olivia Ward gave her highest command scores to the founders she already had context on, meaning the ones introduced through a mentor. Daniel Kim's slot log gives 13 minutes for open-call founders against 21 for introduced. So a criterion meant to test command of the business from live contact may in fact be scoring who got the contact.

Two things I cannot answer yet: what the printed sheet says beside the command line, and whether Daniel's 13 against 21 survives my own recount of the raw log. Both are jobs before I write.

Entrepreneurship   requires   action.   Whether conceptualized   as   the creation   of new   products or  processes   (Schumpeter,   1934), entry   into new markets   (Lumpkin   &   Dess,   1996),  or   the creation of   new   ventures   (Gartner,   1985),   entrepreneur ship   typically   involves   a   mesolevel   phenome non   in which   personal   initiative   influences system-wide   activity   and   outcomes   (Kilby,   1971; Stevenson   &   Jarillo,   1990). o be   an   entrepreneur, therefore,   is to act   on   the  possibility   that one   has identified   an   opportunity   worth   pursuing. Theories   of   entrepreneurship   that   embrace this  perspective   traditionally   have   taken   one   of two   forms. The   first form is devoted   to a   system level   approach   concerned   primarily   with   how the   economic   system   functions.   Proponents   of these   theories   argue   that   the health   of   the econ omy   depends   on   the  pursuit   of  opportunities   by prospective   entrepreneurs   (e.g.,   Kirzner,   1973; Schumpeter,   1934). Who   acts   is   inconsequential as   long  as   someone   does.   Thus,   the central   issue is whether   entrepreneurial   action   occurs.   The second   form   is devoted   to an   individual-level approach   concerned   primarily   with   how   pro spective   entrepreneurs   go   about   acting.   These researchers   seek   to  explain   why   some   individu als   are   more   likely   than   others   to  pursue   possi ble   opportunities   for  profit   (e.g., Begley   &   Boyd, 1987; Sarasvathy,   2001a;   Shane,   2000;   Shaver   & Scott,   1991). Like   before,   entrepreneurial   action takes   center   stage,   but   this   time more   in terms of how   it occurs   and   who   does   it than whether   it  occurs.  The   conceptual   overlap   of   these   approaches suggests   that  they  are   complementary.   In fact, re searchers   of   the   individual-le

vel   approach   have frequently   borrowed   from   theories   grounded   in the   system-level   approach   (e.g.,  Kaish   &   Gilad, 1991). However,   this can   lead   scholars   to  rely  on models   of  entrepreneurial   action   that are   incom plete   when   applied   at   a   level   of  analysis   other than   that   intended   by   the   theorist.  Accordingly, our   purpose   in   this article   is   twofold.   First, we demonstrate   that economic   theories   of   the entre preneur   are   theories   of action   proposing   those   el ements   that enhance   and   hinder   individuals   from acting   entrepreneurial^.   Although   these models may   be   sufficient   for  examining   entrepreneurial action   at   the  system   level,   they  can   collapse   when applied   at   the individual   level, making   them sus ceptible   to confounded   theorizing   and   inconclu sive   or  misleading   empirical   findings.   This   neces sitates   our   second   purpose:   to offer a   perspective that allows   forexamination   of  entrepreneurial   ac tion at   the   individual   level   of  analysis   while   re maining   consistent   with   a   rich   legacy   of  system level   theories   of the  entrepreneur. This   uncertainty   is further enhanced   by   the  novelty   intrinsic   to en trepreneurial   actions   (Amabile,   1997;   Smith   & DiGregorio,   2002),   such   as   the   creation   of new  products,   new   services,   new   ventures,   and   so  forth   (Gartner,   1990;   Schumpeter,   1934).   There fore, it is no   surprise   that  uncertainty   constitutes a   conceptual   cornerstone   for most   theories   of the entrepreneur.   However,   the role   this  uncertainty plays   in  preventing   entrepreneurial   action   has remained   a   matter   of debate.   As   a   result,   two research   streams   have   emerged,   each   inspired by  alternative   conceptualizations   of  uncertainty. The   first stream   focuses   on   the amount   of un certainty   perceived   and   frequently   discrimi nates   those who   decide   to act   entrepreneurial^ from those who   do   not as   a matter   of differences in  knowledge   (e.g., Busenitz,   1996;   Gaglio   & Katz, 2001;   Kaish   &   Gilad,   1991; Kirzner,   1979).   Thus, the amount   of  uncertainty   is   considered   to be the barrier   between   prospective   entrepreneurs and   entrepreneurial   action.   The   second   stream highlights   the  willingness   to bear   uncertainty and   typically   proposes   that   those who   decide   to act   entrepreneurial^   are   distinguishable   from those   who   do   not   owing   to differenc

es   in moti vation,   attitude,   or risk  propensity   (e.g., Douglas &   Shepherd,   2000;   Knight,   1921;   Schumpeter, 1934).   In   this scenario,   an   unwillingness   to bear uncertainty   is deemed   responsible   for  prevent ing prospective   entrepreneurs   from  engaging   in entrepreneurial   action. Because   an   individual   must   ultimately   act   to become   an   entrepreneur,   and   because   action involves   knowledge   and   motivation   (Higgins   & Kruglanski,   2000), we   propose   that each   stream merely   emphasizes   a   different   aspect   of   the un certainty   experienced   in   the   decision   to act entrepreneurially.   Therefore,   each   conceptual ization   of  uncertainty   is  representative   of a   con struct   that   is not  only   reconcilable   with   its coun terpart  but   also   necessary   for further   theorizing about   entrepreneurial   action. By   demonstrating   that   action   is   central   to most   theories   of  entrepreneurship,   we   distill   the various   elements   of action   that must   be   consid ered   concomitantly   when   determining   whether one   will   act   entrepreneurially.   These   include knowledge   (as   it relates   to the amount   of uncer tainty perceived),   motivation   (as   it relates   to the willingness   to bear   uncertainty),   and,   arguably, a   stimulus.   We   propose   that each   of   these   ele ments   produces   a   belief   that   is  qualified   by   un cer

OF THE ENTREPRENEUR  Traditionally,   the   label   theory  of   the  entrepre neur   has   been   used   within   the economics   liter ature   to denote   the   study   of   the   relationship between   entrepreneurship   and   economic   activ ity.  These   theories   (e.g.,   Kirzner,   1973;   Knight, 1921; Schumpeter,   1934)   frequently   attribute   the movement   of   the economy   to a   catalystic   func tion   fulfilled   by   the   entrepreneur.   Accordingly, the   entrepreneur   is   conceptualized   in   terms   of what   he   or   she   does?that   is,   innovates,   coordi nates,   etc.   This   behavior   is   then   thought   to   in fluence   the  system   by moving   it toward,   or  away from, some   ideal   state,   such   as   equilibrium   or efficiency. Two   assumptions   are   characteristic   of most theories   of   the   entrepreneur:   (1) entrepreneur ship   is a   "good"   thing,  with   beneficial   outcomes that   accrue   to   the   system   in which   it occurs  (Kilby, 1971;Stevenson &   Jarillo, 1990),2 and   (2)  entrepreneurship   is   observable   as   a   behavior that   can   be   attributed   to some   definitive   theo retical   attribute   capable   of  differentiating   entre preneur   (actor)   from  nonentrepreneur   (nonactor). Although   the   first  assumption   is   important   for understanding   why   scholars   have   devoted   so much   energy   to the  subject   and   why   the  study   of entrepreneurial   behavior

at   the   individual   level is of value   to  organizational   studies,   it is not   the focal   point   of   this article.   The   second   assump tion, however,   is  highly   significant   to our   argu ment   in   that   it  helps   to  expose   the manner   in which   uncertainty   is   conceptualized   within these   theories. We   suggest   that  many   theoretical   explana tions   of  why   prospective   entrepreneurs   choose to  pursue   a   possible   opportunity   can   be   classi fied   into   two   simple   conceptualizations   of   the role   that  uncertainty   plays   in  preventing   action: (1)   the amount   of  uncertainty   perceived   and   (2) the  willingness   to bear   uncertainty.   We   turn now   to a   deeper   examination   of each. Entrepreneurial   Action   As   the Outcome   of More   Willingness   to Bear   Uncertainty The   theory   of   the  entrepreneur   is not   the ex clusive   domain   of the Austrian   economist.   Prom inent   non-Austrians,   from   Knight   (1921)   to Schumpeter   (1934), also   have   recognized   the role that   uncertainty   plays   in  preventing   entrepre neurial   action.   However,   these   economic   theo rists   conceptualize   uncertainty's   action   prohibi tive   role   in a   slightly   different   way.   They   see entrepreneurial   action   not   as   the   outcome   of less   perceived   uncertainty   but   as   more   willing ness   to bear   the  uncertainty   faced   by   all   pro spective   actors.   For   instance,   Knight   addresses uncertainty   explicitly.   He   posits   that  profit   is the reward   for those  willing   to bear   uncertainty   be cause,   unlike   risk,   uncertainty   is   inestimable and   therefore   uninsurable.   Thus,   entrepreneurs are   distinguishable   from  nonentrepreneurs   in their  willingness   to bear   the  uncertainty   intrin sic   to a   possibly   profitable   course   of action. Because   everyone   in his   economy shares   the same   perceptual   acumen,   opportuni ties must   be   new   to everyone,   not  merely   the actor,   or   else   they  would   already   have   been exploited. However,   its extension   to action   explanation   re quires   one   to determine   whether   the   findings   on how   entrepreneurs   think   they  would   go   about acting   entrepreneurially   correspond   to how   they actually   behave   under   natural   circumstances.14 A  Conceptual   Approach Given   these   various   observations,   we   propose a   conditional   compromise   that   is consistent   with an   action   framework   and   that   includes   eco nomic   theories   of   the   entrepreneur   but   is   not exclusive   to   their  ontological   assumptions.   We argue   that   the  willingness   to bear   the  perceived uncertainty   associated   with   an   entrepreneurial act   is   representative   of a   belief-desire   configu ration,   inwhich   belief   of   what   to do   is a   function of   know

ledge   and   desire   of  why   to do   it   is   a function   of   motivation.   This   conceptualization   is identical   to an   intention   as   described   in the con text of action   theory.   For   instance,   Gr?ve   notes: Actions   are   distinguished   fromother kinds   of hu man   behavior   by   theway   people   usually   explain  how   they   came   about:   They   have   reasons   for ac  tions. This means   that individuals   do what   they do because   they   desire   (want) to reach a  goal   and believe   (expect)   that the action   is an   appropriate  or   necessary   means   of   reaching   it.   The   beliefs and   desires   "rationalize"   the   action   (Davidson,  1980a)   (Gr?ve, 2001: 437).  Given   a   specific   action,   the   presence   of a   specific  intention   (belief-desire   configuration)   cannot   be doubted.   When   an   observed   behavior   is   in fact  the   expression   of   a   certain   action,   then   a   corre  sponding   intention   (constellation   of desires   and beliefs)   is  necessarily   implied;   the  hypothesis  that   this   action   expresses   these   particular   de  sires and   beliefs   cannot   be  disproven   by empiri  cal   means.   The   assertion   that   a   person,   when   he or   she   performs   an   action,   does   so   due   to certain  beliefs   (expectations)   and   desires   (values)   is triv  ially   true,   because   whatever   he   or   she   performs would   not,   in  any   other

case,   be   an   action   (Gr?ve,  2001: 439). Gr?ve   suggests   that   action,   by   definition,   is intentional   behavior.   Therefore,   one   cannot   start with   the   behavioral   portion   of   the   action   and argue   that   increases   in the   intention   caused   the action.   This   would   be   tautological,   given   that the   action   partially   consists   of   the   intention. However,   one   could   avoid   tautology   by   starting with   the  strength   of the   intention   and   predicting whether   the   intended   behavior   subsequently ensues.   Such   an   approach   to  entrepreneurial   ac tion would   equate   the   concept   of   opportunity with   that of   intention. CONCLUSION  We   began   this article   with   an   examination   of the role   that  uncertainty   plays   in economic   the ories   of   the  entrepreneur.   After   establishing   the need   to consider   knowledge   and   motivation   con comitantly   when   examining   entrepreneurial   ac tion,   we   proposed   a   two-stage   conceptual   model of  entrepreneurial   action,   built   on   these   two con structs   and   consisting   of an   attention   stage   fo cused   on   the assessment   of   third-person   oppor tunity   (a possible   opportunity   for someone)   and an   evaluation   stage   focused   on   the assessment of   first-person   opportunity   (a possible   opportu nity   for the actor).   We   then   used   this model   to illustrate   the   conceptual   limitations   of   using system-wide   theories   of   the  entrepreneur   at   the individual   level   of   analysis   by   reinterpreting three economic   theories   considered   highly   influ ential   to  managerial   thought   on   the   subject   of entrepreneurial   action.   Following   this, we   dis cussed   how   the   recognition   that   these   theories of   the  entrepreneur   are   theories   of action,   laden with   ontological   assumptions   about   the   social world,   highlights   the need   for  greater   scholarly attention   to both   knowledge   and   motivation   in future   theory bui

lding   and   empirical   testing.   Fi nally,   we   offered   a   pragmatic   and   a   conceptual solution,   inspired   by   an   action   framework,   as   a means   of  sidestepping   or  acknowledging   philo sophically   intractable   areas   associated   with   the examination   of  entrepreneurial   action. Given   the   renewed   interest   in   the   individual within   entrepreneurship   research   and   the   im portance   of   the   concept   of   opportunity   to   the emerging   field   of  entrepreneurship,   we   believe that scholars   who   employ   these   economic   theo ries   of   the   entrepreneur   will   benefit   from   a deeper   understanding   of   their  predictions,   as sumptions,   limitations,   and   possibilities.   Not only   does   it  appear   that   an   action   framework provides   this   benefit   to  entrepreneurship,   but also   we   believe   that  entrepreneurship   provides a   promising   phenomenon   to extend   scholarly understanding   of   the   economics,   psychology, and   sociology   of human   action.  15 See   Chattopadhyay,   Glick,   and   Huber   (2001)   for an   ex cellent   example   where   they employ   longitudinal   analysis   to examine   the effect   that  perception   has   on   subsequent   action at   the  organizational   level. Coldharbour Launch. Internal memo. From Chloe Park, programme director. To mentors, panel, programme team. Week 7.

Subject: Selection Day scoring sheet, one addition

1. Background. In January the board approved licensing Pitchwright for the spring cohort. The paper to the board (extract below) set the aim: to remove the advantage that founders with prior business vocabulary have had in our written updates, so that Selection Day judges the venture and not the founder's writing.

2. What we have heard. Several mentors report that the weekly updates are now uniform in structure and language and that they are "reading less into them". Two mentors have said they no longer read them before office hours. Founders in the open-call group report shorter office-hours slots than founders introduced through the mentor network (Daniel Kim's slot log, weeks 3 to 6: mean 13 minutes against 21).

3. Change. The Selection Day sheet gains a fifth line, "Founder command of the business", scored 1 to 5, weighted equally with team, market, traction and plan. This makes explicit what mentors say they are already doing in the room. Mentors should score it from their office-hours contact with the founder, not from the deck.

4. Note for the panel. Selection Day decks will still be produced in Pitchwright. Panel members who have not mentored a venture should ask at least one unscripted question before scoring the command line.

Extract, board paper, January. "The evidence from the last two cohorts is that founders who arrive with an MBA, a corporate background or a family business write updates that our mentors rate more highly, and we cannot tell whether the venture or the writing is being rated. A shared writing assistant, required of every founder, levels this. Mentors will be judging comparable documents for the first time."

Programme team note (Daniel Kim, appended week 9). Selection Day results: the three grants went to Kerbside, Bramble (Samuel Price) and Fenwick Labs (Natalie Hayes). All three founders came in through a mentor introduction. Loomly and Tallow, both open call, scored highest on traction and lowest on command. Last cohort, one of three grants went to an introduced founder.

Interview. Olivia Ward, mentor, head of innovation at a regional water utility. Week 6. 42 minutes, her office. Transcript excerpt (cleaned for reading).

MB: How do you prepare for a mentoring slot now, compared with the last cohort?

OW: Last cohort I read the deck the night before and came with questions written on it. This cohort I stopped reading the decks about week three. They are all the same deck. Not similar, the same. Problem statement, then "our wedge", then a traction slide with a hockey stick whether or not there is any traction, then the ask. I know it is the tool because the phrasing repeats. Three ventures used the phrase "underserved by incumbents" in the same week.

MB: So what do you go on instead?

OW: Whether they can hold a conversation about their own business. I ask something that is not on the page and see what happens. The good ones have an answer that is messier than the page. The ones I worry about give me the page back.

MB: Is that a fairer way to judge them, do you think?

OW: Honestly, no. I thought it was, at first. It felt more real. But I have started to notice who does well in that kind of conversation and it is the people who have sat in rooms like this before. Gabriel's been a product manager at a bank, he's fine with being pushed. Hannah is sharp but she gets quieter when you interrupt her and then I don't hear the answer, and I score what I heard.

MB: You said "score". Can you tell me how you filled in the mid-cohort sheet?

OW: There are five lines. Team, market, traction, plan, and the new one, command of the business. Chloe added that one in week seven. I gave the highest command scores to the founders I already had some context on. I mean the ones who had been introduced through someone. Not because I'm biased, because I knew what they'd been doing before the programme, so I could tell when an answer was real. With the open-call ones I only have the room, and the room is fifteen minutes.

MB: What did the programme say the tool was for?

OW: To level things. So a first-time founder with no MBA vocabulary could put a decent page together. Which it does. Their pages are decent. Everybody's pages are decent. That's the problem, the page stopped telling me anything, and I went back to the thing the page was supposed to stop me relying on.

MB: Which is?

OW: Whether they sound like someone I'd back. Whether I know who they are.

Interview. Hannah Foster, founder of Loomly (second-hand school uniform marketplace). Open-call applicant, first venture, previously a primary school teacher. Week 8. 55 minutes, café near the campus. Transcript excerpt.

MB: Tell me about how you use Pitchwright week to week.

HF: I used it properly for the first three weeks, like they asked. You paste in what happened and it gives you the one-pager. It is good. It made me sound like I knew what I was doing. The first week I read it back and thought, that's a real founder's update.

MB: What changed?

HF: Office hours. I'd show Ravi the page and he'd push it away and ask me a question, and the question was never on the page. How many schools, what does a parent pay, why did Bradford say no. I had all that, but not on the page, so I started printing my own page. Just the numbers and what people actually said to me. Two columns. Ugly. That's the page they look at.

MB: So you have two documents each week.

HF: The tool one for the programme, because it's required and Daniel checks that we've submitted it. And mine for the room.

MB: How do the office hours feel?

HF: Short. I get interrupted a lot. Ravi, Olivia, all of them. I know it's a test, they want to see if you can answer. But I was a teacher, when someone interrupts me my instinct is to wait until they've finished and then carry on, and that reads as not having an answer. Gabriel just talks over them. He was in a bank, he says that's normal. I've watched him do it and they seem to like it.

MB: Do you think the tool has made it fairer, the way the programme said?

HF: On paper, yes. I could not have written that page in week one. But nobody reads the page. So what it's done is take away the one thing I could get good at on my own at home, at night, and moved the whole thing into a room where the people who are already comfortable win. I didn't have anyone to introduce me. I came through the website. Gabriel knew Ravi's old finance guy before he walked in.

MB: What would you want the programme to do?

HF: Read the pages. Or stop pretending the pages are the point. Either. Not both at once.

Fieldnote. Coldharbour Launch, mentor office hours, week 4 (Thursday). Room B2, the glass room by the kitchen. 13:40 to 16:10. Marcus Bennett.

Ravi Patel (mentor, sold his logistics software company in 2021) runs office hours with the laptop closed. When I asked before the first slot whether he had read this week's one-page updates he laughed and said "I read three of them in week one and they were the same page with the company name changed. I stopped." He keeps a printed list of the eighteen venture names and writes one word next to each after the slot.

Slot 1, 13:45. Hannah Foster (Loomly, second-hand school uniform marketplace, came through the open call). She opens her laptop to show the update. Ravi waves it away: "Tell me what happened this week." She talks about a school in Bradford that would not sign because the PTA already runs a uniform swap. Ravi interrupts her four times in eleven minutes, each time with a number question (how many schools contacted, how many replied, what does a parent pay now). She has the numbers on a page she printed herself, not the Pitchwright update. He looks at that page. Word written after: "fine".

Slot 2, 14:05. Gabriel Martinez (Kerbside, EV charger booking for terraced streets; introduced to the programme by Ravi's former CFO). Ravi opens with "How's Tom?" (the former CFO). Four minutes on Tom. Gabriel then walks through the Pitchwright update from memory; the structure is the tool's structure (problem, wedge, traction, ask). Ravi interrupts once. Gabriel's answer to "what happened this week" is "we've been refining the go-to-market". Ravi does not press. Word written after: "solid". Slot ran 24 minutes; the slot is 15.

Slot 3, 14:35. Leah Morgan (Tallow, restaurant fat collection; open call, first venture). She has rehearsed the Pitchwright deck and delivers it as a monologue. Ravi lets her finish, then says "Right, now forget all that. What did the restaurant say when you turned up?" She freezes, then tells a story about the kitchen porter being the person who actually decides. Ravi leans forward for the first time in the slot. Word written after: "there's something there".

Between slots Ravi to me, unprompted: "The programme thinks the tool made it fair. It made the pages identical, so now all I've got is the room. And the room is not fair, mate, the room is who's comfortable being interrupted."

Chloe Park (programme director) put her head in at 15:30 to remind mentors that the Selection Day scoring sheet "now has a line for command of the business". Ravi, after she left: "That's the room. They've put the room on the sheet."

Note to self. Count interruptions per slot across mentors next week. Check which founders came in through a mentor introduction: Gabriel, and I think Samuel Price and Natalie Hayes. The open-call founders are getting the shorter slots.

Interview. Gabriel Martinez, founder of Kerbside (EV charger booking for terraced streets). Introduced to the programme by a mentor's former colleague; previously a product manager at a retail bank. Week 8. 38 minutes, the programme's kitchen. Transcript excerpt.

MB: How has Pitchwright been for you?

GM: Brilliant, honestly. It's a time saver. I know what a good update looks like, I've written a hundred of them at the bank, so I paste in my notes and it gives me the shape and I tidy it. Ten minutes. Then I can spend the week on the actual product.

MB: Do the mentors read it?

GM: Ravi doesn't, he's said so. Olivia used to. It doesn't matter much for me, the update isn't where I get anything from them. I get it from the conversation. Ravi knows Tom, my old CFO, so we've got a shorthand. He knows what I did at the bank, so when I say we're refining the go-to-market he knows what I mean by that.

MB: Some of the other founders have said the office hours are hard, the interruptions.

GM: I like it. It's how meetings work. If you can't be interrupted you can't run a company. I'd say that's what the programme should be testing, and it's what they are testing now, with the command line on the sheet.

MB: Did you know about the "level the field" aim, the reason the tool was brought in?

GM: I read it in the welcome pack. Level the field for people who can't write a business page. Which is fair. But the page was never the field. The field is whether people take you seriously in the room, and the tool can't do anything about that. If anything it's cleared the page out of the way so the room is all that's left, which suits me. I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

MB: If Hannah, say, used the tool exactly as you do, would she get what you get from office hours?

GM: No. Not because of the tool. Because Ravi doesn't know anyone she's worked with. It's not the deck, it's the door.

events.text:
This first step is just about grounding the whole study in something real you've actually seen, before we start building any structure around it.

Since you're starting from scratch, let's keep it concrete: what are you looking at right now, in your setting or your data, and what made you stop and think it was worth digging into?

I've been sitting in on a twelve-week pre-seed programme at a university enterprise centre in a northern English city. Spring cohort: eighteen ventures, about forty volunteer mentors, a programme team of three. In January the board licensed an AI writing copilot called Pitchwright and required every founder to write their weekly one-page update and their Selection Day deck in it. The board paper's aim was to level the field between founders who arrive with business vocabulary and first-time founders, so Selection Day would judge the venture and not the founder's writing. What made it worth my time is that within about three weeks the mentors stopped reading the updates. Ravi Patel, one of the mentors, told me he read three of them in week one, they were the same page with the company name changed, and he stopped. So the stated aim and the mentors' actual behaviour pulled apart while I was standing there.

events.rawText:
What I'm exploring is how the stated aim of Pitchwright, to level the field between founders who arrive with business vocabulary and first-time founders, pulled apart from what the mentors actually did within about three weeks. The board licensed the tool so Selection Day would judge the venture and not the founder's writing, but Ravi Patel stopped reading the updates in week one because they were the same page with the company name changed, and he moved the judgment off the artefact and onto the slot instead: office hours with the laptop closed, a printed list of eighteen venture names, one word beside each after the slot. So the thing the board thought would make it fair, made the pages identical and left him with only the room, and as he put it to me, the room is not fair, the room is who is comfortable being interrupted.

Then the sheet itself changed under this: Chloe's week-7 memo adds a fifth line, "Founder command of the business," weighted equally with team, market, traction and plan, scored from office-hours contact rather than the deck. Ravi's reading of that, after Chloe left the room, was that's the room, they've put the room on the sheet. So I'm interested in that move, formalising an in-person, unscripted judgment as a scored criterion equal to the others.

And running under that is the question of who gets read for longer. Olivia Ward told me she gave her highest command scores to founders she already had context on, the ones introduced through someone. Ethan Brooks and Olivia's Slack exchange in week five gestures at the same pattern, and Daniel Kim's slot log turns it into two numbers, 13 minutes for open call against 21 for introduced. So the line meant to test command of the business from live contact may be scoring who had more contact time to begin with, and that time itself may track who was introduced rather than who applied open call.

What I can't answer yet: what the printed sheet says beside the command line, whether there are anchors for 1 and 5 — I have Chloe's memo, not a photograph of the sheet, and I need a blank one from Daniel Kim to check that. And I haven't pulled Daniel's log apart myself, founder by founder across the full twelve weeks, coded by route in — the 13/21 split is his arithmetic and I'm taking it on trust, which I'm not comfortable doing in a paper. My own week-4 timing of Gabriel's slot, 24 minutes against a scheduled 15, is only a partial check against that. Getting the raw log and recomputing it is on my list before I write anything about slot length. [...]

events.subject: starting-interest
events.statement:
A university pre-seed programme required every founder to write their weekly one-page update and their Selection Day deck in an AI writing copilot, Pitchwright, so that Selection Day would judge the venture and not the founder's writing. Within about three weeks that aim and what the mentors actually did pulled apart. Ravi Patel stopped reading the updates in week one because they were the same page with the company name changed, and ran office hours with the laptop closed instead: a printed list of eighteen venture names, one word beside each after the slot. His own gloss was that the tool made the pages identical, so all he has left is the room, and the room is who is comfortable being interrupted.

The programme then wrote the room onto the sheet. Chloe Park's week-7 memo adds a fifth Selection Day line, "Founder command of the business", weighted equally with team, market, traction and plan and scored from office-hours contact rather than the deck. Ravi, after she left: they have put the room on the sheet.

What I want to study is that sequence and who it favours. Olivia Ward gave her highest command scores to the founders she already had context on, meaning the ones introduced through a mentor. Daniel Kim's slot log gives 13 minutes for open-call founders against 21 for introduced. So a criterion meant to test command of the business from live contact may in fact be scoring who got the contact.

Two things I cannot answer yet: what the printed sheet says beside the command line, and whether Daniel's 13 against 21 survives my own recount of the raw log. Both are jobs before I write.

events.question: What was it about Pitchwright specifically that made you choose it as the site for this study, before you'd observed any of the Selection Day judging?
events.reason: The context step needs the reason you picked this setting going in, not the pattern you found once you were there.

events.text:
This step is about pinning down what it was about Pitchwright's setting, before any of the Ravi or Chloe material, that made you think this was the site worth watching.

You've told me a lot already about what happened once you were inside the room, the sameness of the updates, Ravi's shift to interruption tolerance, Chloe's line on the sheet. What I don't have yet is what drew you to Pitchwright in the first place, before you knew any of that would happen.

Small correction first: I did not choose Pitchwright, and Pitchwright is not the site. Coldharbour Launch is the site; the copilot is what arrived in it. I came in with an interest in whether AI writing tools change what expert evaluators attend to, and I was already around the programme as their critical friend.

What made this worth watching was three things that were true before I saw anything happen. The board wrote its aim down in a January paper, before the tool went live, so there is a stated intention I can hold the outcome against. Use was required of all eighteen ventures, so heavy or light use is not a choice that confounds the comparison. And the programme scores every venture on a sheet at a fixed moment, Selection Day, with a previous cohort scored on the same sheet without the tool. That combination is rare. I did not expect the mentors to stop reading.

events.title: Coldharbour Launch is the site, not Pitchwright
events.body: Pitchwright is the copilot, the tool that arrived in the programme. Coldharbour Launch is the programme itself, the site of the study, and you were already around it as critical friend before the tool existed. Worth being precise about this going forward so the ontology doesn't end up organized around the tool's name instead of the site where the tool landed.

events.title: Three things true of Coldharbour Launch before you saw any judging
events.body: The board wrote its aim for the copilot down in a January paper, before it went live, so there's a stated intention on record to hold any outcome against. Use was required of all eighteen ventures, so how heavily a venture used the tool isn't a choice that could confound comparison. And the programme scores every venture on the same sheet at a fixed moment, Selection Day, with a previous cohort already scored on that sheet without the tool in place.

events.question: What was your relationship to Coldharbour Launch, and why that programme specifically, before AI writing tools were part of the question you were asking?
events.reason: You've told me why the setting suits the comparison you want to make, but not what put you inside Coldharbour Launch in the first place, before the copilot or your research question existed.

events.text: Good, that correction matters and I want to hold onto it: Coldharbour Launch is the site, the copilot is what arrived in it, Pitchwright is the tool, not the setting. That changes what "before" means here. You've given me three structural facts, the January paper, the mandatory use across all eighteen ventures, the same-sheet comparison across cohorts, and each is a reason the site is well-suited to answer your question. But none of them is yet a reason you were drawn to Coldharbour Launch specifically, before Pitchwright entered it. You say you were already there as critical friend. What was your relationship to Coldharbour Launch, and why that programme, before AI writing tools were part of the question you were asking?

The honest answer is access rather than theory. I am the programme's critical friend, an informal standing arrangement: I sit in, I feed back, I am not paid and I score nothing. That relationship predates my interest in AI writing tools, and it is why I could be in room B2 on a Thursday afternoon at all.

So I should be plain that this is a convenience sample in the ordinary sense. I did not select Coldharbour Launch from a population of programmes on theoretical grounds. I was already in it when the board licensed Pitchwright in January, and I recognised what that made possible. That is a limitation to write down rather than dress up. It cuts the other way too: the mentors know exactly who I am and what I am there for, so Olivia and Ravi may be performing fairness at me, and I have no clean way to rule that out.

events.title: Critical-friend relationship, unpaid and informal, predates the AI question
events.body: You're in room B2 because you already had standing access to Coldharbour Launch, as an informal critical friend who sits in and feeds back but doesn't score anything and isn't paid. That relationship existed before you had any interest in AI writing tools, and it's the reason you could be there at all when the board licensed Pitchwright. Worth marking as a condition on the whole study: whatever you're seeing is seen from inside a specific, non-evaluative role, not from outside as a neutral observer.

events.title: Convenience sample, access not theory

events.question: Has anyone at Coldharbour Launch, before Pitchwright arrived, pushed back on feedback you gave as critical friend, in a way that shows how much your presence in the room actually influences what people do there?

events.text:
That's a clean admission, and it actually sharpens the site description rather than weakening it. You're not claiming Coldharbour Launch is representative of accelerators generally, you're claiming it's a natural experiment you happened to have standing access to when the licensing decision landed. But that access cuts a specific way I want to pin down: being critical friend means you're in the room, welcomed, presumably with some history of feedback the mentors have heard before. Ravi and Olivia know your prior opinions, not just your role.

Has your critical friend role ever put you in a position where a mentor or the board pushed back on something you said, before Pitchwright, in a way that tells you how much weight your presence actually carries in that room?

Small correction first: I did not choose Pitchwright, and Pitchwright is not the site. Coldharbour Launch is the site; the copilot is what arrived in it. I came in with an interest in whether AI writing tools change what expert evaluators attend to, and I was already around the programme as their critical friend.

What made this worth watching was three things that were true before I saw anything happen. The board wrote its aim down in a January paper, before the tool went live, so there is a stated intention I can hold the outcome against. Use was required of all eighteen ventures, so heavy or light use is not a choice that confounds the comparison. And the programme scores every venture on a sheet at a fixed moment, Selection Day, with a previous cohort scored on the same sheet without the tool. That combination is rare. I did not expect the mentors to stop reading.

The honest answer is access rather than theory. I am the programme's critical friend, an informal standing arrangement: I sit in, I feed back, I am not paid and I score nothing. That relationship predates my interest in AI writing tools, and it is why I could be in room B2 on a Thursday afternoon at all.

So I should be plain that this is a convenience sample in the ordinary sense. I did not select Coldharbour Launch from a population of programmes on theoretical grounds. I was already in it when the board licensed Pitchwright in January, and I recognised what that made possible. That is a limitation to write down rather than dress up. It cuts the other way too: the mentors know exactly who I am and what I am there for, so Olivia and Ravi may be performing fairness at me, and I have no clean way to rule that out.

events.subject: context
events.statement:
Coldharbour Launch is a twelve-week pre-seed programme run by the enterprise centre of a university in a northern English city. The spring 2026 cohort is eighteen ventures, about forty volunteer mentors, and a programme team of three. It ends in Selection Day, where a mentor panel scores every venture on a sheet and three ventures take a 25,000 pound follow-on grant and introductions to an angel syndicate.

In January the board licensed Pitchwright, an AI writing copilot, and required every founder to write their weekly one-page update and their Selection Day deck in it. The board paper's aim was to level the field between founders who arrive with business vocabulary and first-time founders, so that Selection Day would judge the venture and not the founder's writing.

What made me want to study it is that the aim and the mentors' behaviour pulled apart within about three weeks, and I was in the room while it happened. The updates converged in structure and phrasing, mentors stopped reading them, and judgment moved onto the office-hours slot. In week seven the programme wrote that move onto the scoring sheet as a fifth line, "Founder command of the business", scored from office-hours contact rather than from the deck. This is a live case of an AI tool changing what expert evaluators attend to, with the evaluators giving their own account of the shift while it is happening.

Three features make the setting unusually tractable. The aim was written down in a board paper before the tool arrived. Use was required of all eighteen ventures, so heavy or light use is not a self-selected confound. And the same scoring sheet was used on a previous cohort without the tool.

Two things to be honest about. I did not select this site from a population of programmes; I was already its critical friend when the licensing decision landed, so this is a convenience sample. And the mentors know who I am and what I am watching for, so some of what I hear about fairness may be performed at me, and I have no clean way to rule that out.

events.text: You expected "Founder command of the business" to test command of the business from live office-hours contact, weighted equally with team, market, traction and plan. Instead you found Olivia Ward's highest command scores going to founders she already had context on, and Daniel Kim's slot log giving 13 minutes to open-call founders against 21 to introduced ones, so the criterion may be scoring who got the contact rather than command itself.

events.question: What's a piece of the Selection Day judging process you know you don't have visibility into, something that happens when you're not in the room or not being told?
events.reason: The Site step needs you to name not just what your position lets you see, but what it structurally blocks, and "I don't know" here would just mean you haven't located the blind spot yet.

events.text:
This step is about pinning down what your vantage point is good and bad at showing you, given that you're watching from inside a relationship of trust rather than from a neutral position.

You've told me the access is convenience, not selection, and that the mentors know who you are. What I still don't have is a sense of the reverse angle: what does being critical friend keep you from seeing. If Olivia or Daniel are shaping their office-hours behaviour around your presence, or around what they think the sheet is supposed to measure, there may be things happening in that room, or in conversations after you've left, that never reach you because you're the person watching for fairness. What's a piece of the Selection Day judging process you know you don't have visibility into, something that happens when you're not in the room or not being told?

Two big ones. First, the panel deliberation. Selection Day scores are produced jointly: mentors fill in the sheet, but the panel also talks, and what I get is the sheet and whatever people tell me afterwards, not the reasoning as it forms. So when the three grants go to Kerbside, Bramble and Fenwick Labs, I can show you the scores but not the conversation that settled them. Whatever trading or deferring happens between mentors in that room is invisible to me, and individual mentor reasoning is partly hidden inside a joint score.

Second, and upstream: I cannot see what Pitchwright did inside anyone's writing process. I have the outputs, the one-pagers and the decks, and the usage log telling me which ventures used it heavily and which barely. I do not have drafts, prompts, or what a founder pasted in against what the tool handed back. So when Hannah says the first page made her sound like she knew what she was doing, I am taking her word for the mechanism.

events.title: Panel deliberation invisible; joint score hides individual reasoning
events.body: Selection Day scores for Kerbside, Bramble and Fenwick Labs come out of mentors talking to each other, not just filling in a sheet, and what you get afterward is the sheet plus whatever people tell you, not the reasoning as it formed. Any trading or deferring between mentors in that room is invisible to you, and an individual mentor's reasoning is partly folded into a score that's actually joint.

events.title: No visibility into what Pitchwright did inside a founder's writing process
events.body: You have the outputs (one-pagers, decks) and a usage log of which ventures used the tool heavily, but no drafts, no prompts, no record of what a founder pasted in against what the tool handed back. So when Hannah says the first page made her sound like she knew what she was doing, you're taking her word for the mechanism, not observing it.

events.question: What would count as evidence, short of having the actual drafts and prompts, that Pitchwright itself (rather than the founders) is producing the convergence you saw in the one-pagers?
events.reason: You've told me you can't see inside anyone's writing process, so I want to know what indirect trace you think would still let you attribute the sameness to the tool rather than to founders converging on their own.

events.text:
Those two gaps are useful to have named, and they're different in kind. The panel deliberation is missing because you're not in that room. The Pitchwright drafting process is missing because no one, including the founders themselves in some cases, has a record of it. That second one matters more for your puzzle, because "founder command of the business" is being scored partly as a reaction to what the writing looked like, and you can't see the thing that produced the writing.

Given that you only have Hannah's word for what Pitchwright did to her draft, and the outputs plus a usage log for everyone else, what would count as evidence, short of having the drafts themselves, that the tool rather than the founder is doing the work that makes the one-pagers converge in structure and phrasing?

Three things I can actually get at. The previous cohort wrote their updates without the tool and I have those documents and their sheets. If this cohort's pages cluster far more tightly in structure and phrasing than the last cohort's, on the same programme with the same template, that is the strongest evidence available to me.

Second, the usage log splits this cohort into heavy and light users. If convergence tracks how heavily a venture used the tool, that points at the tool. If heavy and light users' pages are equally alike, it points at the programme's template, or at founders copying each other.

Third, signatures. Olivia noticed three ventures using the phrase "underserved by incumbents" in the same week. Phrase-level repetition across ventures that never spoke to each other is hard to explain another way.

None of that is the drafting process. It is convergence measured on the output, with a before-cohort and a dose split. I think that is the best I can do here.

events.title: Three output-side proxies for tool-driven convergence
events.body: Before/after cohort comparison on the same programme and template, a dose split on the usage log (heavy vs light users), and phrase-level signatures like "underserved by incumbents" appearing across ventures with no contact. You're explicit these are all measured on the output, none of them touch the drafting process itself, and you're calling this the best available short of the actual drafts and prompts.

events.title: Same phrase across three unconnected ventures in one week
events.body: Olivia noticed three ventures using "underserved by incumbents" in the same week, ventures that never spoke to each other. You note phrase-level repetition like this is hard to explain another way, without yet saying what it would or wouldn't rule out.

events.question: Is there something within your existing access at Coldharbour Launch, a schedule, shared drive, or founder communication channel, that would let you tell tool-driven convergence apart from founders simply copying each other's language?
events.reason: your three evidence sources are all output-level and venture-level, and I want to know if your site gives you any way to see the process-level alternative explanation you haven't yet ruled out.

events.text: That's a genuinely usable set, and the dose split against a same-template prior cohort is the part I'd defend hardest to a reviewer. But notice what all three of those share: they're measured on the output side, at the level of the venture. None of them tells you whether the convergence is happening because Pitchwright hands every founder similar phrasing, or because founders read each other's updates on the shared drive, or because the programme's own template narrowed everyone toward the same shape before Pitchwright ever touched a sentence. Olivia's "underserved by incumbents" observation is suggestive but it's also compatible with three founders sitting in the same room during a workshop and picking up each other's language. My question about your site now is narrower than the evidence question. Given that you're watching this from inside Coldharbour Launch and not inside Pitchwright, is there a moment or a document in your access, something like a workshop schedule, a shared drive, a founder Slack, where you could actually rule out or confirm founder-to-founder copying as the source of the phrase-level convergence, separate from the tool?

events.question: What is the one sentence you would write into the site section stating what Coldharbour Launch structurally cannot show a reviewer about this puzzle?
events.reason: You've named the gaps in conversation with me, but the site page needs the limit stated as a claim you're willing to stand behind in the paper, not just something you can produce when pressed.

events.text:
Fair enough, that's yours to decline. Let me pull back to what the site question actually needs from you at this point.

You've now given me the two structural gaps (panel deliberation, the drafting process) and a workable evidence strategy for the second one, built entirely on output-side comparisons. What I haven't heard is you naming, in one sentence, what Coldharbour Launch as a site is bad at showing you as a matter of design, not as a thing you might someday fix with cleverer evidence. Every other accelerator running Pitchwright this year would have the same gap. So the question isn't really about this site's limits anymore, it's about whether you can state the limit plainly enough that a reviewer reads it as an honest boundary rather than a hole you're hoping nobody pokes.

If you had to write the one sentence that goes in the site section telling an AMJ reviewer what Coldharbour Launch structurally cannot show them about this puzzle, what would it say?

Here is the sentence. Coldharbour Launch is one programme in one city running one tool with one cohort, and its Selection Day scores are produced by a panel that deliberates in private, so the site can show that mentors' attention moved from the page to the room and who gained by that, but it cannot show that the tool caused the move rather than merely accompanied it, and it cannot show any individual mentor's reasoning apart from the joint score.

I would rather write that plainly than dress it up. What I can defend is a set of within-programme comparisons: this cohort against the last on the same sheet, introduced against open call within the cohort, heavy against light users from the usage log, and mentors' own accounts of the shift given while it was happening. What I cannot offer is a counterfactual programme. A reviewer who wants causal identification should not be reading this paper.

events.title: What the within-programme comparisons can and cannot carry
events.body: The site can support four comparisons and no more: this cohort against last year's on the same sheet, introduced against open-call within the cohort, heavy against light tool users from the usage log, and mentors' own accounts of the shift given while it was happening. What none of these four can produce is a counterfactual programme, so the site cannot show that the tool caused the move from page to room rather than merely accompanied it. You'd rather say this plainly than dress it up: a reviewer who wants causal identification should not be reading this paper.

events.question: Is Selection Day a single fixed scoring event for this cohort, or is there any later point where the scores or the panel's judgment could still shift?
events.reason: Your site sentence covers what one cohort's one Selection Day can and can't show causally, but I want to know whether "one Selection Day" is even a stable unit of observation or a moment inside a process still in motion.

events.text:
That sentence does what it needs to do. You've told a reviewer what mentors' attention did, who gained by the move, and where the causal claim stops, and you've been honest that a counterfactual programme isn't on offer. What it hasn't done yet is say anything about time. Selection Day happens once, at the end of twelve weeks, and you've been in the room for three of those weeks watching the shift start. Coldharbour Launch as a site gives you a single cohort's single Selection Day, and a comparison to a previous cohort's single Selection Day. If something about this move from page to room is still settling, still being negotiated between mentors week to week, a one-shot end point might catch a snapshot of a process that hasn't finished changing.

Is Selection Day itself a fixed, one-time event for this cohort, or is there a later point in the programme, an appeals process, a follow-up panel, anything after the sheet is filled in, where the scoring could still move?

I do not have drafts, prompts, or what a founder pasted in against what the tool handed back. events.subject: site
events.statement:
Why this is the right place. Four things, and they are unusual together. The programme wrote its aim down before the tool arrived, in a January board paper, so there is a stated intention to hold the outcome against rather than one reconstructed afterwards. Use of Pitchwright was required of all eighteen ventures, so heavy or light use is not a choice that confounds the comparison. Every venture is scored on a sheet at one fixed moment, Selection Day, so the judgment is recorded rather than inferred. And a previous cohort was scored on the same sheet without the tool. On top of that the mentors narrate the shift themselves, in office hours, in interviews and in their own Slack channel, while it is happening.

What the place is bad at showing me. Coldharbour Launch is one programme in one city running one tool with one cohort, and its Selection Day scores are produced by a panel that deliberates in private. So the site can show that mentors' attention moved from the page to the room and who gained by that, but it cannot show that the tool caused the move rather than merely accompanied it, and it cannot show any individual mentor's reasoning apart from the joint score.

Upstream of that, I cannot see what Pitchwright did inside anyone's writing process. I have the outputs, the one-pagers and the decks, and the usage log telling me which ventures used it heavily and which barely. I do not have drafts, prompts, or what a founder pasted in against what the tool handed back. So when Hannah Foster says the first page made her sound like she knew what she was doing, I am taking her word for the mechanism.

Two further limits I should state rather than manage. The mentors know I am the programme's critical friend, so some of the fairness talk may be performed at me. And convergence in the pages could come from founders copying each other rather than from the tool. The checks available to me there are all output-side: this cohort's pages against the previous cohort's, heavy users against light users from the usage log, and phrase-level repetition such as the three ventures Olivia Ward saw using "underserved by incumbents" in the same week.

What I can defend is that set of within-programme comparisons plus the evaluators' own accounts. What I cannot offer is a counterfactual programme. A reviewer who wants causal identification should not be reading this paper.
