events.text:
One instance is the evaluation of a single venture across a cohort, and it runs the full twelve weeks. It starts at that venture's first office-hours slot, runs through the weekly one-page update and the mid-cohort sheet, and ends when the panel scores it on Selection Day. So it is founder by founder, eighteen instances running in parallel in this cohort, rather than one programme-wide drift. The drift is real, but it is the condition each instance runs inside, not the process itself.

Inside an instance the repeated unit is the weekly office-hours slot. That is where the judgment is formed and then re-formed: a mentor arrives with an impression, tests it against whatever the founder can do live, writes a word next to the name, and comes back the following week with that word in mind. Ravi's printed list of eighteen names is that process made visible. The written update runs alongside it and, by about week three, stops feeding into it.

events.title: One instance = one venture's evaluation across the full twelve weeks
events.body: You're defining the unit you're tracing as the evaluation of a single venture across the cohort, not any smaller or larger grain. It opens at that venture's first office-hours slot, runs through the weekly one-page update and the mid-cohort sheet, and closes when the panel scores it on Selection Day. That's the span any claim about "how judgment forms" has to hold across, start to end, for it to be about this process rather than some other one.

events.title: Eighteen parallel instances, not one programme-wide drift
events.body: The process you're following runs founder by founder, eighteen separate instances in this cohort running in parallel rather than a single process moving across the whole programme at once. The drift you've confirmed across mentors is real, but you're treating it as the condition each instance runs inside, not as the process itself. So the drift explains the air in the room; it isn't what you're tracing when you follow one venture from office hours to Selection Day.

events.title: Weekly office-hours slot as the repeated unit inside an instance
events.body: Inside a single venture's evaluation, the thing that repeats is the office-hours slot: a mentor comes in holding last week's impression, tests it against whatever the founder can do live, writes a word next to the name, and carries that word into the following week. That cycle, impression tested and re-written, is what does the forming and re-forming across the twelve weeks. The written update runs beside it but you're noting it stops being part of that cycle by around week three.

events.question: Does the page-to-room shift happen at the same point in each venture's own sequence, or does it hit all eighteen instances on the same calendar week regardless of where each one is?
events.reason: You've defined the process as eighteen parallel instances each running its own weekly cycle, but the week-three cutoff you described sounds like a synchronized event, and I need to know which it is before the site section can say what "one instance" actually looks like in time.

events.text:
Good, that's a real answer and it changes the unit. Eighteen parallel instances, each with a repeated weekly beat inside it, that's a lot more tractable than a single cohort-wide drift. But you've now told me two things that sit oddly together: you said the drift is the condition the instance runs inside, not the process itself, and yet you also said the written update "stops feeding into it" by about week three. If that's true for most or all eighteen instances at roughly the same calendar point, that's not a property of one venture's evaluation running its own course, that's a synchronized event hitting eighteen parallel processes at once. Ravi's list makes the office-hours mechanism visible instance by instance, but it doesn't tell me whether week three is something that happens to each venture on its own timeline (say, three weeks after that venture's first office-hours slot) or whether it's a calendar date that hits all eighteen regardless of where each one is in its own cycle.

So: when the page stops feeding into the mentor's judgment for a given venture, is that keyed to something in that venture's own sequence, or does it land on the same calendar week for all eighteen instances regardless of how far along each one is?

That is a fair hit and it changes my answer. The shift is not a property of a venture's own sequence. It happens to the mentor, not to the founder. Ravi stopped reading in week two, Olivia around week three, and in both cases the trigger is having read three or four pages that were interchangeable, which depends on how many they had read rather than on where any single venture sat in its twelve weeks. So it is calendar-like, but keyed to each mentor's own dose of reading rather than to the programme week.

Which means I have two processes and I have been sloppy about it. The venture-level one is what I described: eighteen parallel evaluations over twelve weeks, ending in a score. The mentor-level one is the attention shift, forty of them, each running on its own exposure. They meet in the weekly office-hours slot. I think the mentor-level shift is the process I am actually studying, and the venture evaluation is the unit that carries the outcome.

events.title: Shift keyed to mentor's reading dose, not calendar week
events.body: The move from page to room doesn't line up with programme week and doesn't line up with where a given venture sits in its own twelve weeks either. Ravi stopped reading around week two, Olivia around week three, and in both cases what seems to trigger it is having read three or four pages that felt interchangeable, however many weeks that took. So the clock that matters is each mentor's count of updates read, not the calendar and not the venture's sequence.

events.title: Two processes, previously run together
events.body: You'd been describing this as one thing, eighteen ventures moving through twelve weeks to a score, but you now think there are two processes and you'd been sloppy about which one you're actually studying. The venture-level one is the eighteen parallel evaluations ending in a score. The mentor-level one is the attention shift itself, forty mentors, each running on their own exposure to updates, meeting the venture-level process at the weekly office-hours slot. Your tentative read is that the mentor-level shift is the process you're actually studying, and the venture evaluation is the unit that carries its outcome.

events.question: For the mentor-level process, what is one instance and over what stretch does it run, the full twelve weeks per mentor or a shorter span ending once their reading threshold is crossed?

events.text:
That's a real correction, not just a refinement. You've gone from one process to naming two and then choosing between them, which is exactly the kind of move this step is supposed to force. But notice what you just did to Ravi and Olivia: you gave me their trigger ("three or four interchangeable pages") as if it were the same dose for both, when one stopped at week two and the other at week three. If the mechanism is each mentor's own exposure, then the process you're tracking isn't "mentor attention shifts," it's something with a rate, a count of pages read before the shift happens.

For the mentor-level process you've now decided to study, what's one instance, and what does it run over: is it the full twelve weeks for one mentor across all the ventures they see, or is it something that completes earlier, the span from that mentor's first office-hours slot to the page-count at which they stop reading?

One instance of the mentor-level process runs from that mentor's first read of a weekly update to the point where they stop reading, and in this cohort it does not restart. It is a one-way door. So it is a short span, two to three weeks for Ravi and Olivia, not twelve.

But I want to be careful about the rate. I cannot put a page count on the threshold. What I have is Ravi saying he read three in week one and stopped, and Olivia saying she stopped around week three, and both giving the same reason, that the pages were interchangeable. That is a rate in the loose sense, not a measured dose. To make it a measured one I would need each mentor's reading crossed with which pages they read, and nobody records mentor reading; there is no log of it and I doubt I could reconstruct one honestly. So I would define the instance as first read to stated stopping point, and treat the page count as something I noticed rather than something I measured.

events.title: Mentor-level instance runs first read to stated stopping point, one-way
events.body: For the mentor-level process, one instance runs from that mentor's first read of a weekly update to the point they stop reading, and in this cohort it doesn't restart, so it's a short span rather than the full twelve weeks. For Ravi and Olivia that's roughly two to three weeks. You're defining the instance by first-read-to-stopping-point, not by a fixed calendar window.

That's a rate in the loose sense, but you're careful to say it isn't a measured dose, since a measured one would need each mentor's reading crossed with which pages they actually read. Nobody logs mentor reading, and you doubt you could reconstruct one honestly, so the page count stays something you noticed rather than something you measured.

That's a defensible way to draw the boundary, and I think you're right not to fake a precision you can't back up. Naming it as "noticed, not measured" is honest, and it also tells me something about the instance itself: it's short, it's one-way, and it's defined by a mentor's own report of when they stopped, not by anything external. But that means the instance you've just defined for Ravi and the instance you've defined for Olivia aren't quite the same kind of event, one runs two weeks and one runs three, and you're treating both as "one instance of the mentor-level process" even though you don't know if what happened inside those two spans was the same thing happening at different speeds, or two different things that happen to end the same way. Before I let the length question go, I want to know what's inside the span, not just where it starts and stops.

What actually happens between a mentor's first read and their stopping point, is it a gradual fading of attention across those two or three updates, or is there a specific update, a specific page, where something shifts and the mentor decides the rest aren't worth reading?

Leah Morgan's slot, week four, twenty to three. She had rehearsed the Pitchwright deck and delivered it as a monologue. Ravi let her finish and then said, right, now forget all that, what did the restaurant say when you turned up. She froze. Then she told him about the kitchen porter being the person who actually decides who takes the fat away, and he leaned forward for the first time in the slot.

That is the moment. I had gone in expecting to write about a shared writing tool making documents comparable. What I watched was a mentor deliberately discarding the document the programme had paid to standardise, and getting his best information from the one thing the founder had not prepared. The word he wrote next to her name was "there's something there", the warmest word on his list that afternoon, earned in the two minutes she was off script.

Hannah printing her own ugly two-column page for the room is the same finding from the founder's side.

His note next to her name, "there's something there," was the warmest word he wrote that afternoon, and it came out of the two minutes she was off script.

events.text: That's the sharpest thing you've given me yet, because it's not a description of the shift, it's a scene with a before and an after inside two minutes. Ravi has the deck monologue, then the instruction to forget it, then the freeze, then the kitchen porter detail, then him leaning forward. That's not gradual fading and it's not a threshold crossed silently over three updates, it's a single interaction with a hinge in the middle. Which makes me want to push on something you said a few turns back: that the mentor-level instance runs from first read to stopping point and doesn't restart. Leah's slot is week four. If Ravi already stopped reading pages in week two, then whatever happened in this room with Leah isn't the moment his attention shifts away from the page, that already happened. So what is this scene an instance of instead?

You are right, and it clarifies the whole station. The Leah scene is not an instance of the shift. The shift had already happened to Ravi two weeks earlier. It is an instance of what replaced the page: in-room evaluation, a mentor probing off script and updating a judgment. So I have three things, not two.

One, the mentor attention shift. Short, one-way, over in two or three weeks, and by week four it is finished for Ravi.

Two, the in-room evaluation, which is what the shift produced. One instance is a single office-hours slot: opening, unscripted probe, interruptions, the word written on the list. It repeats weekly, roughly ten times per venture across the cohort.

Three, the venture's evaluation across twelve weeks, which accumulates those weekly words into the mid-cohort sheet and the Selection Day score.

The one I am actually studying is the second, with the first as its origin and the third as where it lands.

events.title: Three processes disentangled: shift, in-room evaluation, venture-level accumulation
events.body: What looked like one thing sorts into three. The mentor attention shift is short and one-way, finished for Ravi by week two. The in-room evaluation is what the shift produced: a weekly office-hours slot with its opening, unscripted probe, interruptions, and the word written down, repeating roughly ten times per venture. The venture's twelve-week evaluation is where those weekly words accumulate, landing in the mid-cohort sheet and the Selection Day score. The Leah scene in week four is an instance of the second, not the first, with the first as its origin and the third as where it lands.

events.title: Which process the study is actually tracking
events.body: The object of study is the in-room evaluation, the weekly office-hours instance, not the attention shift that preceded it and not the twelve-week accumulation that follows it. The shift is treated as origin, the venture-level sheet as destination. Anything the study claims should be read as a claim about this middle process specifically, not about the other two.

events.question: Does every weekly office-hours slot you've observed have the same internal shape as Leah's, an opening followed by a probe that produces the word on the list, or was Leah's slot unusual in making that hinge visible?
events.reason: I need to know if the internal structure you just described is the defining shape of your repeating unit or a feature of one dramatic instance you're at risk of generalizing from.

events.text:
That's a cleaner ontology than you had three turns ago, and I buy the division of labor between the three. The office-hours slot as the repeated unit, with the mentor-shift as its origin condition and the venture-score as its endpoint, gives you something you can actually track across ten repetitions per venture instead of one diffuse drift.

But you've just said "one instance is a single office-hours slot" and then described Leah's slot as having a hinge inside it, the monologue, the instruction to forget it, the freeze, the detail, the lean forward. That's a lot of internal structure for something you're calling one instance of a repeating weekly unit. I want to know whether that hinge structure is Leah's slot specifically or whether it's what a slot is, as a form, for this process. If I asked you to describe a second slot, a different venture, a different week, would it have the same shape: opening, some prepared material discarded or pushed past, a probe, and a word written down? Or was Leah's slot unusual precisely because the hinge was so visible, and most slots don't have one?

The process I'm studying is the in-room evaluation: a mentor probing a founder off script in the weekly office-hours slot and updating a judgment. One instance is a single slot: opening, unscripted probe, interruptions, the word written on the list. It repeats weekly, roughly ten times per venture across the cohort.

It has an origin and a place it lands, and I was sloppy for a while about not separating those from the thing itself. The origin is the mentor attention shift: each mentor reads the weekly written update until it stops giving them anything, and then stops reading it, permanently. That is short and one-way, over in two or three weeks, Ravi stopped in week two, Olivia around week three, and I can't put a page count on the threshold. What I have is each of them saying they'd read a handful of interchangeable pages and quit; that's a rate in the loose sense, not a measured dose, and there's no log of mentor reading to make it a measured one. So I'd define that instance as first read to stated stopping point, and treat the page count as something I noticed rather than something I measured.

Where it lands is the venture's evaluation across the full twelve weeks: one instance is a single venture scored by the panel, running from its first office-hours slot through the weekly update and the mid-cohort sheet to Selection Day. Eighteen of those run in parallel per cohort, forty mentor-level shifts running on their own exposure, and they meet in the weekly slot.

So three processes, three timescales, the shift over two to three weeks, the in-room evaluation weekly, the venture evaluation over twelve, and the one I'm actually following is the middle one.

events.subject: process
events.statement:
The process I am studying is the in-room evaluation: a mentor probing a founder off script in the weekly office-hours slot and updating a judgment. One instance is a single slot, from the opening through the unscripted probe and the interruptions to the word the mentor writes next to the name afterwards. It repeats weekly, roughly ten times per venture across the cohort. Leah Morgan's week-4 slot is a clean instance: the rehearsed Pitchwright deck delivered as a monologue, Ravi saying "right, now forget all that, what did the restaurant say when you turned up", the freeze, the kitchen porter story, and "there's something there" written next to her name.

It has an origin and a place it lands, and I was sloppy for a while about not separating those from the thing itself.

The origin is the mentor attention shift: each mentor reads the weekly written update until it stops giving them anything, then stops reading it, permanently. That is short and one-way, over in two or three weeks. Ravi stopped in week two, Olivia around week three. I cannot put a page count on the threshold; both say they read a handful of interchangeable pages and quit. That is a rate in the loose sense, not a measured dose, and there is no log of mentor reading that would make it one. So I define that instance as first read to stated stopping point, and treat the page count as something I noticed rather than something I measured.

Where it lands is the venture's evaluation across the full twelve weeks: one instance is a single venture, running from its first office-hours slot through the weekly update and the mid-cohort sheet to Selection Day scoring. Eighteen of those run in parallel in this cohort.

So three linked processes: an origin that runs on each mentor's own exposure and finishes early, a repeated in-room evaluation that is the one I am tracking, and a twelve-week accumulation that carries the outcome.

events.text: You expected Pitchwright to level the field so Selection Day would judge the venture rather than the founder's writing, and instead you found mentors abandoning the pages within weeks and writing "Founder command of the business" onto the sheet itself, scored from office-hours contact, with Olivia Ward's highest command scores going to founders she already had context on and Daniel Kim's log showing 13 minutes for open-call founders against 21 for introduced ones.

events.framingDigest: a university pre-seed programme required every founder to write their weekly one-page update and their selection day deck in an ai writing copilot, pitchwright, so that selection day would judge the venture and not the founder's writing. within about three weeks that aim and what the mentors actually did pulled apart. ravi patel stopped reading the updates in week one because events.question: What is the specific comparison in your data whose difference you'd point to as the outcome this study is about?
events.reason: You've described the mechanism in detail but haven't yet said which measured difference, between what and what, stands in for "the outcome" that would make this worth publishing.

events.text:
This step is about pinning down what actually varies at the end of your process, and what change in that thing would tell you the study earned its keep, as opposed to just documenting an interesting shift you happened to be in the room for.

You've given me a lot of texture on the mechanism: mentors stopping reading, the office-hours slot becoming the site of judgment, "Founder command of the business" going onto the sheet. But the sheet has a score, Olivia Ward's and Daniel Kim's scores among them, and behind that a Selection Day outcome, three ventures getting the grant. What I don't yet have from you is which of those levels is the outcome you're claiming varies, and what the comparison is that would let you say it varied. Founder command scores this cohort against founder command scores... what, since that line didn't exist last cohort? Heavy Pitchwright users against light users on the same sheet? Introduced founders against open-call founders, given the Kim log you mentioned?

What is the specific comparison, in your data, whose difference you'd point to and say this is the outcome the study is about?

The outcome is which ventures are selected, and the primary comparison is across cohorts: how far selection tracks prior introduction. That one survives your objection, because it does not need the command line to have existed last time. Last cohort, one of three grants went to an introduced founder. This cohort, three of three: Kerbside, Bramble and Fenwick Labs. Same programme, same grant, same sheet for four of its five lines.

Three supporting comparisons, all within this cohort. Introduced against open call on slot length, Daniel's 21 minutes against 13, on interruption counts, and on the command score. Heavy against light users from the usage log, on how far their pages converged. And the gap between what mentors say they score on the sheet and what they say in the room and on Slack, where Ethan Brooks writes that the pages are all fine and he cannot rank fine against fine.

The result a reviewer should sit up at is Loomly and Tallow: highest on traction, lowest on command.

events.title: Cohort-over-cohort selection rate by prior introduction
events.body: Last cohort, one of three grants went to an introduced founder. This cohort, three of three: Kerbside, Bramble, and Fenwick Labs. This is the comparison you'd point to as the outcome the study is about, and you note it survives the objection that the command line didn't need to exist last time for the pattern to hold. Same programme, same grant, same sheet for four of its five lines.

events.title: Loomly and Tallow diverge on traction and command
events.body: Loomly and Tallow score highest on traction and lowest on command, and you flag this as the result a reviewer should sit up at. You haven't said yet what you think it means, just that it's the pairing in the data that stands out against the rest of the pattern.

events.title: Gap between scored ranking and spoken ranking
events.body: One of your three within-cohort supporting comparisons is the gap between what mentors put on the sheet and what they say in the room or on Slack. Ethan Brooks writes that the pages are all fine and he cannot rank fine against fine. You're holding this as a comparison alongside the introduced-versus-open-call and heavy-versus-light-user comparisons, not yet saying what the gap between stated score and stated difficulty means.

events.question: What would let you attribute the change in selection outcome specifically to mentors abandoning the written page, rather than to the sheet simply acquiring a new line for unrelated reasons?
events.reason: Your primary outcome comparison is across two cohorts where both the tool and the fifth scoring line changed at once, so as it stands the number doesn't yet separate your mechanism from a confound sitting right next to it.

events.text:
That gives me the level, and I like that it doesn't need the command line to have existed last time. But look at what actually differs between the two cohorts you're comparing. Last cohort ran without Pitchwright and without a command line on the sheet at all. This cohort ran with both, introduced in the same twelve weeks, the tool from week one and the fifth line from week seven. So when you point to 1 of 3 grants going to an introduced founder last time against 3 of 3 this time, you have two things moving together between your two data points, not one. A reviewer could read that shift as evidence the tool changed what mentors attend to, or just as easily as evidence that the fifth line itself, whatever produced it, changed the scoring in a way that has nothing to do with reading behavior on the page. You can't currently tell those apart from the cross-cohort number alone, since you only have one cohort on each side of the comparison and both changes happen at once.

What would let you attribute the shift in who gets selected specifically to mentors abandoning the page, rather than to the sheet simply having a new line on it that any programme might have added for other reasons?

Partly I can and partly I cannot, and it matters which.

What I can show is the ordering, and it is documented rather than reconstructed. Mentors stopped reading in weeks two and three. The fifth line arrived in week seven. Chloe's memo gives its own reason under "What we have heard": several mentors report the updates are uniform and that they are reading less into them, and two say they no longer read them before office hours. So the sheet change is downstream of the abandonment by the programme's own account. The line did not appear for unrelated reasons; it was written to catch what mentors were already doing.

That closes the unrelated version, not the harder one. If I strip the command line out and rescore this cohort on the four lines the last cohort also had, and the introduced founders still come top, the story is bigger than the new line. If they do not, and Loomly and Tallow scoring highest on traction suggests they may not, then the fifth line carries the difference, and my claim shrinks to this: the tool emptied the page, the programme wrote the room onto the sheet, and the sheet did the rest. I would rather find that out than assert around it. Two cohorts on each side would settle it and I do not have them.

events.title: Chloe's memo dates the abandonment before the fifth line
events.body: The memo's "What we have heard" section has several mentors reporting the updates are uniform and that they're reading less into them, and two saying they no longer read them before office hours. That account puts the abandonment before the fifth line arrived in week seven, and the programme's own record is that the line was written to catch what mentors were already doing. So the ordering isn't something you're reconstructing after the fact, it's what the programme itself says happened.

events.title: Strip the fifth line and rescore on the old four
events.body: If you take the command line out and rescore this cohort on the four lines the last cohort also had, and the introduced founders still come out on top, the effect is bigger than the new line and your claim about abandonment holds more broadly. If they don't, and Loomly and Tallow scoring highest on traction is a hint they might not, then the fifth line is carrying the difference, and what you can claim shrinks to a specific chain: the tool emptied the page, the programme wrote the room onto the sheet, and the sheet did the rest. You haven't run this yet, but it's the test that would tell you which version you're in.

events.title: Two cohorts each side would settle it, and you don't have them
events.body: Even with the strip-test result, you'd want two cohorts before the abandonment and two after to be confident the pattern isn't cohort-specific noise. You're working with one cohort on the new side of the line, so whatever the rescoring shows, it settles the mechanism for this instance without yet settling whether it generalizes.

events.question: If you ran the four-line rescoring today using the scores you already have, what do you expect it would show, introduced founders still on top or not?
events.reason: You've named the test as the thing that would settle your claim, and I want to know whether you already have a working guess from the data in front of you or whether this is still genuinely open.

events.text: This is the right instinct, and I want to press on the design it implies rather than let it sit as a hypothetical. You've described a falsification test, rescore this cohort on the four old lines only, see if introduced founders still come out on top. That test either shrinks your claim to "the fifth line carries the difference" or expands it to "the whole sheet was already retilted." But you don't yet have the four-line rescoring done, and until you do, you don't actually know which outcome variable you're defending: selection under all five lines, or selection under the four shared lines. Those are different claims with different evidentiary bars, and right now you're holding both open at once.

My honest expectation is that they would not still be on top, or only narrowly. Loomly and Tallow scored highest on traction of the eighteen and both came through the open call, and traction is one of the four shared lines. If traction is where the open-call ventures are strongest and command is where they are weakest, a four-line rescoring probably narrows the gap a long way and may reverse at least one of the three grants.

I am writing that expectation down now, before I run it, because I do not trust myself to remember it afterwards.

And I should be honest that this is the outcome that makes the paper smaller. The finding then is not that AI writing tools bias selection. It is that a required writing tool emptied the artefact of information, the programme responded by scoring the interaction instead, and the criterion it added is the one that tracks prior acquaintance. That is narrower and I think truer. It also puts the causal weight on the programme's response rather than on the tool, which is not what I set out expecting.

events.title: Programme's response to an emptied artefact, not tool bias
events.body: If the rescoring goes the way the researcher expects, the account they're now sitting with is that the required writing tool emptied the artefact of information, and the programme responded by scoring the interaction instead of the writing. The criterion it added to compensate is the one that happens to track prior acquaintance. The researcher is explicit that this puts the causal weight on the programme's response rather than on the tool, and that this is narrower than what they set out expecting, but they think it's truer.

events.question: Which outcome would you put in the abstract as the thing that varied, the selection result under the rescoring or the mentors' own reports that the instrument stopped discriminating?
events.reason: You've now given me evidence for two different outcome variables in the same breath, a scoring result and a reported evaluative failure, and the paper can lead with only one of them.

events.text:
What you just laid out is honest in a way that matters, and I want to sit with the smaller finding for a second rather than let it slide past. If the four-line rescoring narrows or reverses the grants, the outcome you're claiming isn't "who wins" anymore, it's something upstream of that, the criterion itself and where it came from. But you've also given me a second thing in the same paragraph: Ethan Brooks saying the pages are all fine and he can't rank fine against fine. That's a mentor telling you the instrument failed for him specifically, independent of any score. So I'm no longer sure whether your outcome variable is the selection result (who gets the grant), or the scoring behavior that produces it (what mentors say they can and can't do with the sheet), and those two would need different evidence to move.

If you had to point to only one of those, either the selection result after the four-line rescoring, or the pattern of mentors saying the instrument stopped discriminating for them, which one is the outcome you'd put in the abstract as the thing that varied?

Both, in a fixed order, and I would put them in the abstract in that order. The thing that varied is the selection result: three of three grants to introduced founders against one of three in the previous cohort. That is the outcome the programme cares about and the reason anyone reads past the first page.

The mentors' reports that the instrument stopped discriminating are the mechanism, not a second outcome. Ethan Brooks saying he cannot rank fine against fine is the hinge that explains why the selection result moved. Without it I have a correlation between a tool and a cohort. Without the selection result I have an interesting complaint.

So the outcome is which ventures are selected, and on what grounds mentors say they judged. The grounds half is not decoration; it is the only part that says why, and it is the part I can evidence best, because the mentors say it in three registers: to me in interview, to each other on Slack, and to Chloe in the memo that changed the sheet.

events.title: Selection result as outcome, discrimination collapse as mechanism, in that order
events.body: You're splitting the abstract into an outcome and a mechanism, and putting them in a fixed order: selection result first, then mentors' account of why. The selection result is what varied, three of three grants to introduced founders against one of three in the previous cohort, and that's the number the abstract leads with because it's the reason anyone keeps reading. The discrimination-collapse reports aren't a second outcome sitting alongside it, they're the explanation for why the first number moved.

events.title: Outcome without mechanism is correlation, mechanism without outcome is complaint
events.body: You said the two pieces need each other to mean anything: the selection result alone gives you a correlation between a tool and a cohort, and the mentors' account alone gives you an interesting complaint. It's only holding both, the number and the reason mentors give for the number, that gets you something worth calling a finding. You're naming this as the reason the grounds half of the claim isn't decoration.

events.title: Discrimination-collapse claim recurs across interview, Slack, and memo
events.body: You can evidence the "instrument stopped discriminating" claim in three separate registers: mentors saying it to you in interview, mentors saying it to each other on Slack, and mentors saying it to Chloe in the memo that changed the scoring sheet. You're flagging this as the part of the mechanism claim you can back most solidly, because it shows up unprompted across three different audiences rather than only in the setting where you asked for it.

events.subject: outcome
events.statement:
The outcome is which ventures are selected, and on what grounds mentors say they judged. For the study to be worth doing I need to see differences in four places.

Across cohorts, in how far selection tracks prior introduction. Last cohort one of three grants went to an introduced founder. This cohort three of three: Kerbside, Bramble and Fenwick Labs. Same programme, same grant, same sheet for four of its five lines.

Within this cohort, between introduced and open-call founders: slot length, where Daniel Kim's log gives 21 minutes against 13, interruption counts, and the command score.

Within this cohort, between heavy and light users of the tool from the usage log, in how far their pages converged. That is the check that separates the tool from the programme's template or from founders copying each other.

Between what mentors say they score and what they say they actually do: the sheet against the room and the Slack channel, where Ethan Brooks writes that the pages are all fine and he cannot rank fine against fine.

The single result a reviewer should sit up at is Loomly and Tallow, both open call, highest on traction and lowest on command.

The confound I have to handle. Two things changed between the cohorts, not one: the tool arrived in week one and the fifth line in week seven. What I can show is the ordering, and it is documented rather than reconstructed. Chloe's memo says under "What we have heard" that mentors report the updates are uniform and that they are reading less into them, and that two no longer read them before office hours. The sheet change is downstream of the abandonment by the programme's own account, so the line did not appear for unrelated reasons.

What that does not close is whether the fifth line carries the whole difference. The test is to rescore this cohort on the four lines the previous cohort also had. I am recording my expectation before running it: I expect the introduced founders would not still be on top, or only narrowly, because Loomly and Tallow are strongest on traction, which is one of the four shared lines.

If that is what it shows, the claim shrinks and I will let it shrink. It becomes: a required writing tool emptied the artefact of information, the programme responded by scoring the interaction instead, and the criterion it added is the one that tracks prior acquaintance. That puts the causal weight on the programme's response rather than on the tool, which is not what I set out expecting. Two cohorts on each side would settle it and I do not have them.

events.text: You expected Pitchwright to level the field so Selection Day would judge the venture and not the founder's writing, and instead you found the programme writing a "Founder command of the business" line onto the sheet that Olivia Ward scores highest for founders she already had context on, and that Daniel Kim's log gives 13 minutes to open-call founders against 21 to introduced ones. A criterion meant to test command of the business from live contact may in fact be scoring who got the contact.

events.question: What is your unit of collection, and does it give you enough cases on both sides of the introduced/open-call line and the heavy/light-use line to make those comparisons rather than just gesture at them?
events.reason: The comparisons you've built your outcome claims around (introduced vs open-call, heavy vs light users) only hold if your sample has real variation on those two dimensions, and you haven't yet told me what you're collecting as your unit or how many fall on each side.

events.text:
This step is about naming who and what you're actually collecting, precisely enough that a reader can see it's a sample built to hold a comparison, not just everyone you happened to have access to at Coldharbour.

You've told me a lot about processes and outcomes, but not yet who's in the sample. You've named individuals as instances (Leah Morgan's week-4 slot, Ravi's stopping point, Ethan Brooks's remark) and you've named group contrasts (introduced versus open-call, heavy versus light users, this cohort versus last). Those contrasts only hold if the people and artefacts you're collecting actually vary along the lines the comparison needs. Eighteen ventures, forty mentors, three programme staff, two cohorts of scoring sheets, a usage log, Slack messages: that's the population available to you, but the sample is whatever subset of that you're actually pulling in as data.

What are you including as your unit of collection, every venture and mentor pairing across all twelve weeks, or something narrower, and does that unit give you enough ventures on both sides of the introduced/open-call line and both sides of the heavy/light-use line to make those comparisons rather than just gesture at them?

Two units, and I should have said so earlier. The venture is the unit for anything I can count: all eighteen ventures' weekly updates, their Pitchwright usage figures from the log, and their Selection Day sheets, plus the previous cohort's sheets on four of the same five lines. That is a census of the cohort rather than a sample, and it covers both sides of the route-in line, roughly a third introduced through a mentor and two thirds through the open call. The second unit is the office-hours slot, which is where the judgment actually gets made, and that one is a sample: about thirty slots observed across four mentors over ten weeks. For interviews I picked seven founders to fill cells. Hannah Foster and Leah Morgan open call, Gabriel Martinez, Samuel Price and Natalie Hayes introduced, crossed with heavy and light use from the log. Crossed both ways at once the cells are one or two deep. That is thin and I would rather say so than dress it up.

events.title: Census at venture level, sample at office-hours and interview level
events.body: The venture is a census, all eighteen ventures' updates, usage logs and Selection Day sheets, so the introduced/open-call split (roughly a third to two thirds) is covered in full at that level. The office-hours slot is a different unit and a sample, about thirty slots across four mentors over ten weeks, and the interview set is smaller still, seven founders picked to fill cells. So whatever the venture-level data can support on its own, the same comparison run through office-hours observation or interviews is resting on much thinner numbers, and I shouldn't let the census cover for the sample when I write this up.

events.title: Interview cells crossed on route-in and use-intensity are one or two deep
events.body: I picked seven founders to fill cells crossing introduced/open-call with heavy/light Pitchwright use: Hannah and Leah for open call, Gabriel, Samuel and Natalie for introduced. Crossed on one dimension the groups are workable, but crossed on both at once each cell holds only one or two founders. I'd rather flag that thinness now than let the interview material carry more weight than seven people split into four cells can hold.

events.question: How are the thirty observed slots distributed across the four mentors, and does one or two of them account for most of what you observed?
events.reason: If your mechanism claim (mentors' attention shifting) rests on a slot sample dominated by one or two mentors, you're generalizing a four-mentor programme's behavior from what might be one or two people's habits.

events.text:
Good, that's the distinction I was missing. The venture census settles the countable comparisons, but the slot sample is a different animal, and thirty slots across four mentors is where the command score and the interruption counts actually come from. Four mentors is also the group whose attention shift, Ravi's week two, Olivia's week three, is doing a lot of the explanatory work in your account. If two of those four turn out to carry most of the thirty slots, or if the introduced/heavy-use cell only has coverage from one mentor, your claim about mentors' attention shifting stops being a claim about the process and starts being a claim about a couple of people who happened to be watched most.

How are the thirty slots distributed across the four mentors, roughly evenly, or does one or two of them account for most of what you observed?

Skewed, and you have put a finger on the weak spot. I am there two afternoons a week and Ravi Patel's Thursday office hours is the one I have never missed, so he carries something close to half the thirty slots on his own. Olivia Ward I have watched six or seven times, Ethan Brooks four or five, and the fourth mentor is a corporate innovation lead who does one afternoon a month. So the attention shift I can document as observation is really Ravi's: week two, laptop closed, one word written next to each name. Olivia's week-three shift I have from her interview, not from sitting in it, and Ethan's I only have from the Slack channel, where he says he still reads the updates and cannot rank fine against fine. Which means in the observed slots the introduced and heavy-use founders are mostly Ravi's founders, and I cannot pull the mentor apart from the cell. The fix is to watch Olivia and Ethan deliberately for the weeks I have left.

events.title: Mentor confounded with cell for introduced/heavy-use founders
events.body: The founders who are introduced and heavy-use are mostly Ravi's founders in your observed slots, so you can't tell whether what you're seeing is a mentor effect or a route-in/use-intensity effect. Ravi's week-two shift (laptop closed, one word per name) is something you watched directly; Olivia's week-three shift you only have secondhand from her interview; Ethan's account of still reading and not being able to rank fine against fine you only have from Slack. Three different evidence types standing in for what should be the same kind of observation across mentors, and you can't yet separate the mentor from the cell.

events.question: Of the slots you've already observed for Olivia and Ethan, how do they split across the introduced/open-call and heavy/light-use lines?
events.reason: I need to know whether adding their weeks actually fills the empty cells or just adds a second mentor's data to cells Ravi already dominates.

events.text:
That's a clean admission, and it tells me the fix isn't just "watch more slots," because Ravi's founders and the introduced/heavy-use founders overlap in ways you haven't separated yet. If Olivia's six or seven slots and Ethan's four or five happen to sit mostly on the open-call or light-use side, watching them more this term doesn't rebalance the cell, it just gives you a second mentor's version of the same imbalance.

Of the slots you've already watched for Olivia and Ethan combined, roughly how many fall on introduced founders versus open-call, and heavy versus light use?

I have not counted it, which is the honest answer, and it is countable because every fieldnote names the founder in each slot alongside the start time. So that is an afternoon's work with the fieldnotes and the usage log, not new fieldwork, and I will do it before I write the sample section. What I can say from memory is that Olivia's slots skew open-call, because she took the Tuesday group and the open-call founders were mostly assigned there, and Ethan's are the ones he cut short. If that holds, you are right that watching them more does not rebalance anything. The cell that stays empty either way is introduced plus light user, and I am not sure there is a founder in this cohort who sits in it.

events.title: Olivia and Ethan's slots, recalled split by route-in and use
events.body: Uncounted so far, but from memory: Olivia's slots skew open-call because she took the Tuesday group and that's where the open-call founders mostly landed, and Ethan's slots are the ones he cut short. This is recall, not a tally, and you're treating it as provisional until you run the count against the fieldnotes and usage log. If it holds once counted, watching Olivia and Ethan more doesn't rebalance the introduced/open-call or heavy/light split, it just gives you more of the same skew.

events.title: Introduced-plus-light-user cell may be empty in this cohort
events.body: The cell that stays empty either way, introduced founder paired with light tool use, may simply have no occupant this cohort. You're not sure a founder exists who sits in it. If so, any claim your design makes about that cell can't be tested here regardless of how the count comes out, and that's a limit on the comparison, not a finding about it.

events.question: Does the introduced/light-use cell exist anywhere among all eighteen ventures in the usage log, even outside your interview sample?
events.reason: If that combination doesn't exist in the cohort at all, your two central comparisons collapse into one and I want you to know that before you write the sample section, not after.

events.text:
That's a real gap to name, not just a coverage problem. If introduced-plus-light-user doesn't exist as a lived combination in this cohort, then heavy use and being introduced are confounded at the level of who the founders are, not just at the level of who you happened to watch. That would mean your heavy/light comparison and your introduced/open-call comparison might be tracking the same underlying split rather than two independent lines of variation, which changes what either comparison alone can tell you.

Have you checked the usage log against the introduction status for all eighteen ventures to see whether that empty cell is a fact about the cohort, or just a gap in the five founders you picked for interview?

events.question: Can you pull the usage log and cross it against introduction status for all eighteen ventures to see whether the introduced/light-use cell is empty across the whole cohort, not just your five interviewees?
events.reason: You've named this as the fact that would tell you whether heavy use and being introduced are one underlying split or two independent ones, and it's sitting in data you already have rather than data you'd need to go collect.

events.text: Fair enough, and I'd rather you say that than guess. This is a fact sitting in the venture-level census you already have, not something that needs new fieldwork: eighteen ventures, each with an introduction status and a usage figure from the log. Checking it is a matter of sorting the spreadsheet you already described having.

For the venture-level data, the variation is already there since it's a census of the cohort: all eighteen ventures, both sides of the route-in line, roughly a third introduced through a mentor and two thirds through the open call.

For the office-hours slots, the comparison I want is between introduced and open-call founders, and between heavy and light Pitchwright use, crossed against each other. For that to hold, the thirty observed slots need to actually vary on those two things independent of which mentor is running the slot. Right now they don't, the attention shift I can document is really Ravi's, and in the observed slots the introduced and heavy-use founders are mostly his founders. So I cannot pull the mentor apart from the cell, which means the comparison doesn't hold yet.

What the sample needs, then, is Olivia's and Ethan's slots represented with enough weight, and specifically representing the cells that are thin, introduced founders and heavy users, not just more of what they already have. But I said Olivia's slots skew open-call and Ethan's are the ones he cut short, so if that holds, watching them more doesn't rebalance anything; it just adds more open-call, mentor-specific variation rather than the introduced/heavy-use variation I need.

And the cell that has to be there for the four-way comparison to hold at all, introduced plus light user, may not be fillable, because I'm not sure there is a founder in this cohort who sits in it. [...]

For the interviews, crossed both ways at once the cells are one or two deep, which is thin for making the comparison I want across route-in and usage together.

events.subject: sample
events.statement:
The sample has to vary on three things for the comparisons to hold: route into the programme (introduced through a mentor against the open call), prior business vocabulary (corporate, MBA or family business against a first venture), and Pitchwright use (heavy against light, from the usage log). The previous cohort supplies the fourth line of variation, the same sheet without the tool.

There are two units. The venture is the unit for anything countable, and there the variation is already present because it is a census rather than a sample: all eighteen ventures' weekly updates, their usage figures, and their Selection Day sheets, plus the previous cohort's sheets on the four shared lines. Roughly a third of the eighteen came in introduced, two thirds through the open call. The office-hours slot is the second unit and the one where the judgment is actually formed, and that is a sample: about thirty slots across four mentors over ten weeks. Seven founder interviews were chosen to fill cells, Hannah Foster and Leah Morgan open call, Gabriel Martinez, Samuel Price and Natalie Hayes introduced, crossed with heavy and light use.

Three weaknesses I have to state rather than manage. First, the slot sample is mentor-weighted: Ravi Patel's Thursday office hours carries close to half of it, so the attention shift I can document as observation is his. Olivia Ward's I have from her week-six interview and Ethan Brooks's only from the Slack channel. In the observed slots the introduced and heavy-use founders are mostly Ravi's founders, so mentor and cell are not separable yet. Second, Olivia's slots skew open-call and Ethan's are the short ones, so simply watching them more adds coverage without rebalancing the cells. Third, introduced plus light user may not exist as a lived combination in this cohort, which would mean route in and usage are confounded in who the founders are, not merely in who I watched, and neither comparison could then stand alone.

Two things I can settle without new fieldwork, and will before I write this section: cross-tabulate the observed slots by mentor, route in and usage from the fieldnotes, which name the founder and start time for every slot, and check the usage log for whether the introduced/light cell exists across all eighteen. Crossed both ways at interview level the cells stay one or two deep, and I will report them that way.

events.text: You expected the fifth line, "Founder command of the business," to test something the fifth line's own design promises, live command shown in office hours. Instead you found Olivia Ward's highest command scores going to founders she already had context on, and Daniel Kim's slot log giving 13 minutes to open-call founders against 21 to introduced ones, so the criterion may be scoring who got the contact rather than who has command.

events.paperName: mcmullen-shepherd-2006.pdf
events.framingDigest: a university pre-seed programme required every founder to write their weekly one-page update and their selection day deck in an ai writing copilot, pitchwright, so that selection day would judge the venture and not the founder's writing. within about three weeks that aim and what the mentors actually did pulled apart. ravi patel stopped reading the updates in week one because they were the same page with the company name changed, and ran office hours with the laptop closed instead: a printed list of eighteen venture names, one word beside each after the slot. his own gloss was that the tool made the pages identical, so all he has left is the room, and the room is who is comfortable being interrupted. the programme then wrote the room onto the sheet. chloe park's week-7 memo adds a fifth selection day line, "founder command of the business", weighted equally with team, market, traction and plan and scored from office-hours contact rather than the deck. ravi, after she left: they have put the room on the sheet. what i want to study is that sequence and who it favours. olivia ward gave her highest command scores to the founders she already had context on, meaning the ones introduced through a mentor. daniel kim's slot log gives 13 minutes for open-call founders against 21 for introduced. so a criterion meant to test command of the business from live contact may in fact be scoring who got the contact. two things i cannot answer yet: what the printed sheet says beside the command line, and whether daniel's 13 against 21 survives my own recount of the raw baselines.expectation: New organizations whose founders start with prior ties to a network's members receive more early contact, attention, and resource flow from that network than founders without such ties.
baselines.scope: Stated for founders and new organizations at or near founding, drawing on network position at the time of entry into a resource environment.

baselines.expectation: Differences in initial network position persist over time because early access begets further access, so a founder who starts with more contact accumulates a compounding advantage rather than the gap closing on its own.
baselines.scope: Stated as a dynamic unfolding over the early life of the organization, not claimed to reverse absent some intervening structural change.

events.title: Uniform pages stop mentors from reading them
events.body: Multiple mentors independently report the weekly Pitchwright updates have become interchangeable and they've stopped reading them, which is the opposite of what a legibility tool is supposed to produce. Olivia Ward says "They are all the same deck. Not similar, the same" and names the repeated phrase "underserved by incumbents" [[chunk:5424432e-5339-4bc4-89b7-d146dfac7507]]. Ravi Patel says he read three in week one and stopped [[chunk:f98ca04f-f097-4baf-afa8-c5b90e832ac3]], and Chloe Park's own memo confirms "several mentors report... they are reading less into them" [[chunk:092ca834-03bb-4eea-8682-bc9c84fadd04]].

events.title: Introduced founders get longer office-hours slots
events.body: Daniel Kim's slot log shows introduced founders averaging 21 minutes against 13 for open-call founders across weeks 3 to 6 [[chunk:092ca834-03bb-4eea-8682-bc9c84fadd04]], and this shows up live in the fieldnote where Gabriel's slot runs 24 minutes against a scheduled 15 while Hannah and Leah get compressed slots [[chunk:28e11f01-cc47-4ee3-87b2-0596e8a144d2]]. Ethan Brooks names the same pattern about himself: "Gabriel's slot ran 25 mins again. Leah got 11 because I had to leave. Not proud of that" [[chunk:d6d50f0b-9d17-4537-be6e-96abc3e3f3a1]].

events.title: Tool removed writing as a signal, mentors substituted room performance
events.body: Olivia Ward gives the clearest first-person account of the mechanism: the pages became decent for everyone, "the page stopped telling me anything, and I went back to the thing the page was supposed to stop me relying on," which she names as "whether they sound like someone I'd back" [[chunk:533ae601-1f69-4b1b-b9f9-65271b196667]]. Ravi Patel states the same causal chain to Marcus directly: "It made the pages identical, so now all I've got is the room. And the room is not fair, mate, the room is who's comfortable being interrupted" [[chunk:28e11f01-cc47-4ee3-87b2-0596e8a144d2]]. Chloe Park's memo formalizes this substitution by adding a "command of the business" line scored from office-hours contact [[chunk:092ca834-03bb-4eea-8682-bc9c84fadd04]].

events.title: Command-of-business score tracks prior exposure to being interrupted, not venture quality
events.body: Olivia admits she scored command highest for founders she already had context on "because I knew what they'd been doing before the programme, so I could tell when an answer was real" [[chunk:533ae601-1f69-4b1b-b9f9-65271b196667]]. Gabriel, a former bank product manager, says being interrupted "is how meetings work" and endorses the command line as testing the right thing [[chunk:48c3ba91-ac43-48d1-9089-28fe91d4c87d]], while Hannah Foster, a former teacher, says interruption "reads as not having an answer" for her [[chunk:6da43e6d-6dd5-4b69-ab42-ea802ed3321c]]. This suggests the command score may be measuring rehearsed comfort with a particular conversational style rather than command of the venture itself.

events.title: It's the door, not the deck
events.body: Gabriel offers a competing account of what actually drives the disparity: not the tool's removal of writing as signal, but pre-existing relationships between mentors and introduced founders. Asked whether Hannah would get what he gets if she used the tool identically, he says "No. Not because of the tool. Because Ravi doesn't know anyone she's worked with. It's not the deck, it's the door" [[chunk:da5a5470-8def-41b3-b088-d9ba83098d5e]]. This locates the cause in the introduction network itself rather than in anything the tool changed.

events.title: Hannah Foster keeps two documents each week
events.body: Hannah describes maintaining the required Pitchwright one-pager for the programme alongside a self-made two-column page of "the numbers and what people actually said to me" that she actually uses in the room, because office-hours questions are "never on the page" [[chunk:8daaf22d-d44d-4ed4-b2b8-5fe0d2123984]]. This is directly corroborated in the fieldnote, where Ravi waves away her laptop and looks instead at the page she printed herself [[chunk:f98ca04f-f097-4baf-afa8-c5b90e832ac3]].

events.title: Selection Day grants went entirely to introduced founders
events.body: Daniel Kim's appended note records that all three Selection Day grants (Kerbside, Bramble, Fenwick Labs) went to founders who came in through a mentor introduction, while the two highest-traction open-call ventures, Loomly and Tallow, scored lowest on the new command line [[chunk:f87f37d1-6bf1-4222-8416-cc791b5ef700]]. The note also flags that last cohort, before the tool and before the command line, one of three grants went to an introduced founder, an implicit before/after contrast.

events.title: Ravi runs office hours with the laptop closed
events.body: The fieldnote records Ravi Patel keeping a printed list of eighteen venture names and writing one word next to each after a slot, having stopped reading the Pitchwright updates after week one because "they were the same page with the company name changed" [[chunk:f98ca04f-f097-4baf-afa8-c5b90e832ac3]]. His one-word notes across three consecutive slots ("fine", "solid", "there's something there") are the only visible trace of his scoring process in the field record [[chunk:28e11f01-cc47-4ee3-87b2-0596e8a144d2]].

events.title: Gabriel endorses the very asymmetry that disadvantages him least
events.body: Gabriel states the command-of-business line is "what the programme should be testing, and it's what they are testing now" [[chunk:48c3ba91-ac43-48d1-9089-28fe91d4c87d]], while also acknowledging in the same interview that the tool "cleared the page out of the way so the room is all that's left, which suits me. I'm not going to pretend otherwise" [[chunk:da5a5470-8def-41b3-b088-d9ba83084d5e]]. His endorsement of the fairness of the current arrangement sits alongside his explicit self-interest in it, and the material doesn't resolve whether his account of what the programme "should" test is a genuine belief or a rationalization.

events.title: Chloe Park frames the command line as making explicit what mentors already do
events.body: Chloe's memo describes the new scoring line as making "explicit what mentors say they are already doing in the room" [[chunk:092ca834-03bb-4eea-8682-bc9c84fadd04]], treating the room-based judgment as a pre-existing, presumably legitimate practice being formalized. This framing sits in tension with Ravi's characterization of the same change, "They've put the room on the sheet" [[chunk:f98ca04f-f097-4baf-afa8-c5b90e832ac3]], which reads as diagnosing a problem rather than endorsing a fix, and with Olivia's own admission that her room-based judgments are shaped by prior familiarity rather than what happens in the fifteen minutes [[chunk:533ae601-1f69-4b1b-b9f9-65271b196667]].

events.question: What did you find in your material that you didn't expect and that doesn't simply confirm the introduced-versus-open-call pattern you already had in mind?
events.reason: The early-data step is meant to surface a genuine surprise in the material itself, not a restatement of the hypothesis you brought to the field, and I want to know if something in your data has pushed back on your own framing.

events.text:
This step is about what your material has put in front of you that you weren't looking for when you went in, the thing you noticed rather than confirmed.

You've already told me a lot about the pattern you expected to find (command scores tracking prior acquaintance, slot time skewed toward introduced founders). But Olivia's interview has something in it that doesn't fit neatly into that story: she says the room "felt more real" at first, and only later did she start to notice who does well in it. That's a mentor narrating her own judgment changing shape over time, not just a mentor confirming a bias you'd already hypothesized.

What did you find in the material, in a fieldnote, a transcript, a memo, that you didn't go looking for and that doesn't just confirm the introduced/open-call story you walked in with?

Three things I did not expect. The first is that the mentors stopped reading the page rather than reading it differently. I went in expecting polished, comparable pages to be judged more alike. Olivia put it as everybody's pages being decent and that being the problem, and Ethan Brooks on Slack could not rank fine against fine. Nobody predicted that a levelling tool would empty the artefact out.

The second is that the programme then wrote the room onto the sheet. Chloe Park's week-7 memo adds "Founder command of the business" and says in terms that it makes explicit what mentors are already doing. That is an organisation formalising the thing the intervention was supposed to remove, in writing, within seven weeks.

The third is the one that unsettles my own story rather than confirming it. Loomly and Tallow scored highest on traction and lowest on command, so the founders with the best evidence about their businesses were the ones the new criterion punished. And Gabriel Martinez, who benefits, says it out loud and defends it: it is not the deck, it is the door. I expected the advantaged founder to be unaware of the advantage. He is completely aware and thinks the room is the right test.

events.question: Is there any instance in your material of an introduced founder scoring low on command, or an open-call founder scoring high, something that cuts against the pattern you've just described?
events.reason: I want to know whether the mechanism you're building holds only in the cases you've foregrounded, or whether you have a case that resists it too.

events.text:
Gabriel defending the room as the right test is the one I'd sit with longest. It means the founder who benefits most from the shift isn't hiding behind a naive story about merit, he has a competing theory of what should count as evidence, and it isn't obviously wrong. That's harder to write around than an unaware beneficiary would be.

But I want to ask about the edges of your own pattern now, not the center of it. You've given me three things that don't fit your original hypothesis but do fit each other, mentors stopping reading, the programme formalizing the room, and the traction/command split for Loomly and Tallow. Is there anything in the transcripts, fieldnotes, or Slack that runs against that cluster too, an introduced founder who scored low on command, or an open-call founder the room actually rewarded?

The nearest thing I have is Leah Morgan, and it is a near miss rather than a counter-case. She is open call, first venture, and she delivered the Pitchwright deck as a rehearsed monologue, which is the failure mode. Then Ravi said forget all that, what did the restaurant say when you turned up, and she told him about the kitchen porter being the person who actually decides. That is the only moment in my week-4 fieldnote where Ravi leans forward, and the word he wrote afterwards was "there's something there", which is warmer than the "fine" he gave Hannah. So the room did open for an open-call founder once, when the question stopped being a question about the page. Her command score still came out low.

On the other side I have not checked. Daniel's note gives me Loomly and Tallow at the top on traction and the bottom on command, but I have not read the command line for the fifteen other ventures individually, and it is entirely possible one of the three grant winners scored poorly on command and won on team or market. I should tabulate that before I claim the pattern is clean, because right now I am arguing from two founders and an aggregate.

events.title: Leah Morgan's room opened, her command score didn't follow
events.body: The one moment in your week-4 fieldnote where Ravi leans forward for an open-call founder is Leah's, when the question stops being about the page and she tells the kitchen-porter story. He writes "there's something there," warmer than the "fine" he gives Hannah [[chunk:28e11f01-cc47-4ee3-87b2-0596e8a144d2]]. But her command score still came out low, so the room opening didn't carry through to the score the way your account would predict. You're calling this a near miss rather than a counter-case, and I'd leave it exactly that unsettled: it doesn't overturn the pattern, but it isn't absorbed by it either.

events.title: Pattern currently rests on two founders and one aggregate line
events.body: Right now the claim that introduced founders score high on command and open-call founders score low draws on Hannah, Gabriel, and Daniel's note that Loomly and Tallow sit lowest on command and highest on traction [[chunk:f87f37d1-6bf1-4222-8416-cc791b5ef700]]. You haven't read the command line for the other fifteen ventures individually, and you said yourself one of the three grant winners could have scored poorly on command and won on team or market. Until that tabulation is done, the pattern holds at the level of two founders and an aggregate, not a checked census.

events.question: Is there an open-call founder in the untabulated fifteen who scored high on command despite having no prior acquaintance with their mentor?
events.reason: Gabriel's account suggests comfort-under-interruption could reward founders independent of the introduction route, and I want to know if your material has a case that would separate those two explanations rather than only ones that fold into your pattern.

events.text:
That's the right discipline, catching yourself arguing from two founders and an aggregate rather than the full set. Gabriel's "it's not the deck, it's the door" also gives you a clean prediction to test against, if the room really does reward comfort-with-interruption regardless of route in, you'd expect to find at least one open-call founder who's simply good at being pushed and scores well on command for that reason, not because of prior acquaintance. That would be a different kind of complication than Leah, one where the mechanism you've been tracking (introduction giving mentors context) turns out to be one path among others to a high command score, not the only one.

Have you looked at the fifteen ventures you haven't tabulated yet for a founder who fits that shape, open call, no prior context with the mentor, but scoring high on command anyway?

events.question: In the office-hours slots you've personally observed, is there any open-call founder who got a warm command-type word from a mentor without the mentor having outside context on them first?

Setting aside the fifteen you haven't tabulated, in the slots you've actually sat in on, Ravi's especially, is there a single open-call founder who got a warm word from him, "solid" or better, on a slot where he didn't already have some outside context on them, the way he did with Gabriel and Tom?

I should tabulate that before I claim the pattern is clean, because right now I am arguing from two founders and an aggregate.

events.subject: early-data
events.statement:
Four things the material has shown me that I did not go in expecting.

Mentors stopped reading the page rather than reading it differently. I expected polished, comparable updates to be judged more alike. Instead Olivia Ward stopped at about week three because everybody's pages were decent and that was the problem, Ravi Patel stopped in week two after three updates that were the same page with the company name changed, and Ethan Brooks kept reading and found he could not rank fine against fine. A tool brought in to make the artefact comparable made it uninformative.

The programme then wrote the room onto the sheet. Chloe Park's week-7 memo adds "Founder command of the business", scored from office-hours contact rather than the deck, and says in terms that this makes explicit what mentors are already doing. Within seven weeks the organisation formalised the thing the intervention was meant to remove, in writing, and said so.

The founders with the best evidence were the ones the new criterion punished. Loomly and Tallow scored highest on traction and lowest on command. I had assumed command and substance would at least point the same way.

The advantaged founder is not unaware of his advantage. I expected Gabriel Martinez to tell a merit story. He does not: he says the page was never the field, that the tool has cleared the page out of the way so the room is all that is left, which suits him, and that it is not the deck, it is the door. He also thinks the room is the right test. That is a competing theory of what should count as evidence, held by the person it favours, and it is not obviously wrong.

What cuts against the pattern, and what I have not checked. The one moment the room opened for an open-call founder is Leah Morgan's week-4 slot: she delivered the Pitchwright deck as a monologue, Ravi told her to forget it and asked what the restaurant actually said, and she gave him the kitchen porter. That is the only point in that fieldnote where he leans forward, and he wrote "there's something there" rather than the "fine" Hannah got. Her command score still came out low. On the other side I have not read the command line for the fifteen ventures I did not interview, so I cannot yet rule out an introduced founder scoring badly on command, or an open-call founder scoring well simply because they are comfortable being interrupted. Gabriel's account predicts the latter should exist. Until I tabulate all eighteen I am arguing from two founders and an aggregate, and I will say so rather than round it up.
