events.question: Of Olivia, Ravi, and Chloe, whose felt pull between two demands they can't reconcile do you think should anchor this paper?
events.reason: each of them is caught between a different pair of things, and the bind you build the paper around has to be one person's lived contradiction, not your synthesis of the pattern across all three.

events.text:
This step is about naming the pull that the people in your setting can't resolve for themselves, not the one you're constructing across your data. So far you've given me your bind: the board's language versus the room's practice, a gap you can see because you're standing outside both.

What I don't yet have is anyone inside Coldharbour saying they feel pulled between two things they can't reconcile. Olivia comes closest. She tells you the room "felt more real," then in the same breath tells you she scores command from prior context, then says "honestly, no" when you ask if that's fairer. That's not her reporting a finding to you, that's her catching herself mid-sentence. Ravi's line, "not blaming the tool, and then we rank on something else, and the something else is worse," has the same shape: he names the trade without being able to stand outside it.

So when you write this up, whose bind is it? Is it Olivia's, having to score a document she knows is empty against a room she doesn't trust herself in? Is it Ravi's, who thinks he's fixed a problem and thinks he's made it worse in the same sentence? Or is it Chloe's, writing a memo that formalizes the very thing the board paper was written to prevent, and saying so in writing? Those are three different people caught between two different things, and the paper can probably only carry one of them as its center.

None of the three, and I think the question has left out the people who pay for it. Olivia, Ravi and Chloe are all caught, and Chloe's is the sharpest institutionally, but all three of them have somewhere to stand. They can name the trade, they get to keep their jobs either way, and Ravi in particular can say the room is not fair and then carry on running it.

The bind that should anchor the paper is Hannah Foster's, because she cannot name it and cannot escape it. She is required to file the Pitchwright page, and Daniel checks that she has. She knows nobody reads it. So she writes a second page by hand, two ugly columns of numbers and what people actually said, for the room. She is complying and routing around the compliance in the same week, and doing double the work to do it. Her own account of the cost is precise: the tool took away the one thing she could get good at on her own, at home, at night, and moved the whole thing into a room where the people who are already comfortable win.

That is a bind, not a dilemma someone is observing. And it has an artefact: the two documents. Leah Morgan is the same bind without the workaround, which is why her deck comes out as a monologue.

events.title: Hannah Foster's bind anchors the paper, not a mentor's dilemma
events.body: Olivia, Ravi, and Chloe are all caught between the tool and what it costs, but each of them can name the trade out loud and keeps the job either way, Ravi can say the room isn't fair and carry on running it the next day [[chunk:5424432e-5339-4bc4-89b7-d146dfac7507]]. Hannah cannot name it and cannot get out of it: she is required to file the Pitchwright page, Daniel checks that she has, she knows nobody reads it, so she writes a second page by hand for the room, complying and routing around the compliance in the same week [[chunk:8daaf22d-d44d-4ed4-b2b8-5fe0d2123984]]. That's what should anchor the paper, a bind someone is living rather than a dilemma someone with standing is observing.

events.title: Leah Morgan as the same bind, minus the workaround
events.body: Leah Morgan is in Hannah's position, required to file the tool's page, judged on something the page doesn't carry, but she hasn't built the second document Hannah built for herself. Without that workaround she delivers the Pitchwright deck straight, as a rehearsed monologue, and only breaks from it when Ravi forces the question the page can't answer [[chunk:28e11f01-cc47-4ee3-87b2-0596e8a144d2]]. She's the control case for what the bind looks like with no artefact routing around it.

events.question: What exactly is it that Hannah can't name, given that she can already describe the cost of the shift in those terms?
events.reason: You're building the center of the paper on her being caught without language for it, and I want to know what's missing from what she's already said.

events.text:
That reframe changes what the paper has to explain. If it's Hannah's bind, the tension isn't between two things the programme wants, it's between compliance and the thing compliance was supposed to replace, and she's building the workaround herself with no one asking her to. Olivia at least gets to say "honestly, no" out loud, to you, in a room where that costs her nothing. Hannah's second page never gets said out loud to anyone who scores her.

But I want to press on "cannot name it." You've told me what she does about the bind, the two documents, and what she says it costs her, "moved the whole thing into a room where the people who are already comfortable win." That's a pretty precise naming. What is it you think she can't name, if she can say that much?

Fair, I overstated it. She names it better than I do. What she has no place to say it is the thing I should have written.

She said it to me in a cafe, in week eight, off the record as far as she is concerned. There is no forum at Coldharbour where that sentence counts as input. The weekly update is the channel, and the channel is the thing she is complaining about. Office hours are fifteen minutes and she spends them being interrupted about parent pricing. The Selection Day sheet has no line for it. So she can describe the trap precisely and still have nowhere to put the description, which is why it comes out as a second sheet of paper instead of a complaint.

And her actual ask is one the programme cannot grant on its own terms: read the pages, or stop pretending the pages are the point, either, not both. Granting the second half means conceding the board paper was wrong within a term. That is the bind underneath hers, and it is why nothing moves.

Office hours are fifteen minutes of being interrupted about parent pricing, not a place to make the argument [[chunk:8daaf22d-d44d-4ed4-b2b8-5fe0d2123984]]. The Selection Day sheet has no line for it either, so she can state the trap precisely and still have nowhere at the programme to put the statement, which is why it comes out as a second sheet of paper instead of a complaint [[chunk:6da43e6d-6dd5-4b69-ab42-ea802ed3321c]].

events.title: Hannah's ask is two things the programme can't grant together
events.body: Read the pages, or stop pretending the pages are the point, either one, not both [[chunk:6da43e6d-6dd5-4b69-ab42-ea802ed3321c]]. Granting the second half means conceding, within a single term, that the board paper's stated aim (level the field so mentors judge the venture, not the writing) was wrong. That's the bind underneath her bind, and it's my current best sense of why nothing moves, though I haven't got past naming it that way.

events.question: Is there any place in your material where Chloe Park herself names the contradiction between the board paper's promise and her own memo's admission, or is that connection something only you have drawn?
events.reason: you've identified the bind underneath Hannah's as institutional, and I want to know whether it lives in anyone's account inside Coldharbour or only in your analysis of the documents.

events.text: That's the sharpest version of it yet, because it locates the impossibility not in Hannah's psychology but in the programme's own contradiction. The board paper says the tool levels the field. Chloe's memo says the room is what mentors are already doing, in effect admitting the deck doesn't count. Those can't both be true, and granting Hannah's ask, either read the pages or stop pretending they matter, forces the programme to pick one and lose the other. But you've named this as the bind underneath Hannah's, the institutional one. I want to know whether it's actually hers to carry, or whether it belongs to someone with the authority to grant or refuse that ask. Chloe wrote the memo that formalizes the room. She's the one who could, in principle, read the pages or drop them. Does she talk or write about that choice anywhere, or is the only person who names the underlying contradiction you, sitting outside both documents?

She does, once, in writing, and it is the single most useful line I have. In the mentors' Slack channel in week five, after Daniel posts the slot log showing 21 minutes against 13, Chloe writes that she is proposing a line on the Selection Day sheet so that we are at least scoring the room openly rather than pretending we score the deck. That is the programme director naming the contradiction herself, in the channel, before she writes the memo.

What is interesting is what happens to that sentence between the channel and the memo. On Slack it is an admission that the deck is a pretence. In the week-7 memo it becomes "this makes explicit what mentors say they are already doing", which is the same fact with the pretence taken out and the fairness aim left standing. She never retracts the board paper. So the contradiction is named once, informally, and then absorbed into procedure.

Which answers your question in a way I had not put together until now: it is not that only I can see it. Chloe saw it first and solved it by writing it onto the sheet, and that act is what converted a mentor habit into a scored criterion.

events.title: Chloe's Slack admission becomes the memo's fairness claim
events.body: In week 5, after Daniel posts the slot log, Chloe writes in the mentors' Slack channel that she is proposing the command line "so we are at least scoring the room openly rather than pretending we score the deck" [[chunk:d6d50f0b-9d17-4537-be6e-96abc3e3f3a1]]. That is her naming the contradiction herself, informally, before any memo exists. By the week-7 memo the same move is described as making "explicit what mentors say they are already doing" [[chunk:092ca834-03bb-4eea-8682-bc9c84fadd04]], the same fact with the word "pretending" gone and the board paper's fairness aim left standing, unretracted.

events.question: Is there a moment where a mentor is put in the position of having to choose between saying the Slack-honest version of the shift and the memo-safe version, in a setting where that choice would have cost them something?
events.reason: You've shown me Chloe absorbing her own contradiction into procedure without cost to herself, and I want to know whether that same move, informal truth traded for formal fiction, is something only the director can do, or whether a mentor faces it too.

events.text:
That distinction between the Slack sentence and the memo sentence is the whole mechanism in miniature. Chloe writes "pretending we score the deck" to the mentors, and writes "makes explicit what mentors say they are already doing" to everyone else. Same fact, but one version can still be said out loud and the other can't. That gives you two audiences for the same admission, and it makes me wonder whether the bind actually sits with Chloe alone or whether it's structural to her position, something any programme director would hit once a mentor posts a slot log like Daniel's.

Chloe named the contradiction once, informally, before she had to solve it in writing. Is there a moment where a mentor, not Chloe, is asked to choose between the Slack version and the memo version, where saying the informal thing in a formal setting would have cost them something?

events.question: Who currently holds an expectation about this setting, and what do they expect to happen?
events.reason: Something is only a puzzle if it unsettles somebody's expectation, so say whose. [asked past saturation: 0 change to your models in the last 8 turns]

events.text:
The Slack thread gives you Chloe's move in real time, and it settles something you'd been circling for three turns without quite landing it. Now I want to step back from Hannah and Chloe specifically and ask about the fuller cast.

Who currently holds an expectation about this setting, and what do they expect to happen?

Five parties, and they expect incompatible things.

The board holds the strongest and the most documented one. Their January paper says mentors rate founders with an MBA or corporate background more highly, that they cannot tell whether the venture or the writing is being rated, and that a shared writing assistant required of everyone levels this. The sentence they commit to is that mentors will be judging comparable documents for the first time. That is the expectation my case breaks.

Chloe holds a version of it and defends it in week five: if the pages are all fine, that is the tool working. She is right on the tool's own terms and wrong about what follows.

The mentors expected the room to be the more honest instrument. Olivia says it felt more real at first. She has since revised, and when I asked whether it was fairer she said honestly, no.

Hannah expected the page to be the part she could get good at on her own, at home, at night. Gabriel expected nothing from the page and everything from the conversation, and got both.

And I held one: that comparable pages would be judged more alike. Nobody in the setting expected mentors to stop reading altogether, and that is the expectation whose failure the paper turns on.

events.title: Board's leveling expectation for the shared writing tool
events.body: The board's January paper commits to a specific claim: mentors couldn't tell whether the venture or the writing was being rated, and a shared writing assistant required of every founder levels this, so mentors will be judging comparable documents for the first time [[chunk:f87f37d1-6bf1-4222-8416-cc791b5ef700]]. You name this as the strongest and most documented expectation held by anyone in the setting, and the one your case breaks. You don't yet say what replaces it, only that this is the expectation whose failure the paper turns on.

events.title: Chloe's week-five defense: uniform pages mean the tool is working
events.body: In the mentors channel, Chloe answers Olivia and Ethan's complaint that the pages are all "fine" and can't be ranked against each other by saying that's the tool working, since it was brought in so the writing wouldn't be the thing being ranked [[chunk:d6d50f0b-9d17-4537-be6e-96abc3e3f3a1]]. You say she's right on the tool's own terms, and wrong about what follows, without yet specifying what that further wrong thing is. This sits as a live alternative reading of the same fact (uniform pages) that you and she draw opposite conclusions from.

events.question: Does any of the five people or parties hold a stated belief about what actually makes a venture worth funding, apart from their expectation about how the scoring process will register it?
events.reason: I want to know if the bind is only about the instrument of judgment, or whether it also splits people on what judgment is even for.

events.text:
This is the widest the cast has looked all session, and it's useful precisely because the five expectations don't stack, they cross. The board expects comparable documents. Chloe expects the tool is "working" when pages go flat. The mentors expected the room to be more honest and at least one of them, Olivia, has already taken that back out loud. Hannah expected the page to be hers alone to get good at. You expected comparable pages to read as more alike. And Gabriel is the only one whose expectation and outcome still match, which is its own fact.

But I notice you've stated what each of them expects to happen, not what any of them thinks is actually true about founders or ventures independent of the programme. The board's sentence is a prediction about mentors' future behavior. Olivia's "it felt more real" is a claim about the room as an instrument. Those are expectations about the evaluation process itself, not about what makes a venture good. I want to know whether any of your five hold a belief about entrepreneurial merit, what actually makes Kerbside or Loomly worth funding, that's separate from their expectation about how Selection Day will judge it.

None of the three, and I think the question has left out the people who pay for it. Olivia, Ravi and Chloe are all caught, and Chloe's is the sharpest institutionally, but all three of them have somewhere to stand. They can name the trade, they get to keep their jobs either way, and Ravi in particular can say the room is not fair and then carry on running it.

events.subject: bind
events.statement:
Three binds, nested, and the one that should anchor the paper is the founders'.

The founders are caught between complying with a required tool that makes them sound like everyone else, and going off-script to be seen, which risks reading as unprepared. Hannah Foster resolves it by doing both and paying twice: the Pitchwright page for the programme, because Daniel checks it has been submitted, and a second page she writes by hand, two ugly columns of numbers and what people actually said, for the room. That is the bind with an artefact attached. Her own account of the cost is exact: the tool took away the one thing she could get good at on her own, at home, at night, and moved the whole thing into a room where the people who are already comfortable win. Leah Morgan is the same bind without the workaround, which is why her week-4 slot comes out as a rehearsed monologue.

What makes it a bind rather than a grievance is that she has nowhere to put it. The weekly update is the channel, and the channel is what she is complaining about. Office hours are fifteen minutes and she spends them being interrupted about parent pricing. The sheet has no line for it. She said it to me in a cafe in week eight and nowhere else. And her actual ask is one the programme cannot grant on its own terms: read the pages, or stop pretending the pages are the point, either, not both. Granting the second half concedes the board paper was wrong inside a term.

The mentors are caught between the fairness aim they were given and their sense that the page no longer tells them anything, so they fall back on the room and on who they know. Olivia Ward is the clearest case: she says the room felt more real, then that she gives her highest command scores to founders she already had context on, then that she went back to the thing the page was supposed to stop her relying on, and when I asked whether it was fairer she said honestly, no. Ravi Patel holds both halves in one sentence: not blaming the tool, and then we rank on something else, and the something else is worse.

Chloe Park is caught between the board's promise and a result that looks worse on the promise's own terms. Her bind is visible in what one sentence becomes between two audiences. On Slack in week five, to the mentors, she proposes the new line so we are at least scoring the room openly rather than pretending we score the deck. In the week-7 memo, to everyone, the same fact reads: this makes explicit what mentors say they are already doing. The pretence is edited out and the fairness aim is left standing, and the board paper is never retracted. So the contradiction is named once, informally, and then absorbed into procedure. That act is what turned a mentor habit into a scored criterion.

Who feels the pull hardest: the open-call founders, Hannah and Leah, and after them the mentors who have noticed what they are doing, Olivia and Ravi. Gabriel Martinez is the one person whose expectation and outcome still match, and he is not caught at all, which is itself a finding.

events.title: Uniform pages stop mentors from reading them
events.body: Multiple mentors independently report the weekly Pitchwright updates have become interchangeable and they've stopped reading them, which is the opposite of what a legibility tool is supposed to produce. Olivia Ward says "They are all the same deck. Not similar, the same" and names the repeated phrase "underserved by incumbents" [[chunk:5424432e-5339-4bc4-89b7-d146dfac7507]]. Ravi Patel says he read three in week one and stopped [[chunk:f98ca04f-f097-4baf-afa8-c5b90e832ac3]], and Chloe Park's own memo confirms "several mentors report... they are reading less into them" [[chunk:092ca834-03bb-4eea-8682-bc9c84fadd04]].

events.title: Site warrant: aim on record before the tool, use required of all eighteen, same sheet across two cohorts
events.body: The board wrote its aim for the copilot down in a January paper, before it went live, so there's a stated intention on record to hold any outcome against. Use was required of all eighteen ventures, so how heavily a venture used the tool isn't a choice that could confound comparison. And the programme scores every venture on the same sheet at a fixed moment, Selection Day, with a previous cohort already scored on that sheet without the tool in place.

events.title: Critical-friend relationship, unpaid and informal, predates the AI question
events.body: You're in room B2 because you already had standing access to Coldharbour Launch, as an informal critical friend who sits in and feeds back but doesn't score anything and isn't paid. That relationship existed before you had any interest in AI writing tools, and it's the reason you could be there at all when the board licensed Pitchwright. Worth marking as a condition on the whole study: whatever you're seeing is seen from inside a specific, non-evaluative role, not from outside as a neutral observer.

events.title: Panel deliberation invisible; joint score hides individual reasoning
events.body: Selection Day scores for Kerbside, Bramble and Fenwick Labs come out of mentors talking to each other, not just filling in a sheet, and what you get afterward is the sheet plus whatever people tell you, not the reasoning as it formed. Any trading or deferring between mentors in that room is invisible to you, and an individual mentor's reasoning is partly folded into a score that's actually joint.

events.title: No visibility into what Pitchwright did inside a founder's writing process
events.body: You have the outputs (one-pagers, decks) and a usage log of which ventures used the tool heavily, but no drafts, no prompts, no record of what a founder pasted in against what the tool handed back. So when Hannah says the first page made her sound like she knew what she was doing, you're taking her word for the mechanism, not observing it.

events.title: Same phrase across three unconnected ventures in one week
events.body: Olivia noticed three ventures using "underserved by incumbents" in the same week, ventures that never spoke to each other. You note phrase-level repetition like this is hard to explain another way, without yet saying what it would or wouldn't rule out.

events.title: What the within-programme comparisons can and cannot carry
events.body: The site can support four comparisons and no more: this cohort against last year's on the same sheet, introduced against open-call within the cohort, heavy against light tool users from the usage log, and mentors' own accounts of the shift given while it was happening. What none of these four can produce is a counterfactual programme, so the site cannot show that the tool caused the move from page to room rather than merely accompanied it. You'd rather say this plainly than dress it up: a reviewer who wants causal identification should not be reading this paper.

events.title: Shift keyed to mentor's reading dose, not calendar week
events.body: The move from page to room doesn't line up with programme week and doesn't line up with where a given venture sits in its own twelve weeks either. Ravi stopped reading around week two, Olivia around week three, and in both cases what seems to trigger it is having read three or four pages that felt interchangeable, however many weeks that took. So the clock that matters is each mentor's count of updates read, not the calendar and not the venture's sequence.

events.title: Stopping rate noticed, not measured
events.body: You have Ravi saying he read three updates in week one and stopped, and Olivia saying she stopped around week three, both citing the same reason, that the pages were interchangeable. That's a rate in the loose sense, but you're careful to say it isn't a measured dose, since a measured one would need each mentor's reading crossed with which pages they actually read. Nobody logs mentor reading, and you doubt you could reconstruct one honestly, so the page count stays something you noticed rather than something you measured.

events.title: Leah Morgan's week four slot, twenty to three
events.body: Leah delivered her Pitchwright deck as a rehearsed monologue. Ravi let her finish, then told her to forget all that and say what the restaurant had actually said when she turned up. She froze, then told him about the kitchen porter deciding who takes the fat away, and that was the point he leaned forward for the first time in the slot. His note next to her name, "there's something there," was the warmest word he wrote that afternoon, and it came out of the two minutes she was off script.

events.title: Three processes disentangled: shift, in-room evaluation, venture-level accumulation
events.body: What looked like one thing sorts into three. The mentor attention shift is short and one-way, finished for Ravi by week two. The in-room evaluation is what the shift produced: a weekly office-hours slot with its opening, unscripted probe, interruptions, and the word written down, repeating roughly ten times per venture. The venture's twelve-week evaluation is where those weekly words accumulate, landing in the mid-cohort sheet and the Selection Day score. The Leah scene in week four is an instance of the second, not the first, with the first as its origin and the third as where it lands.

events.title: Which process the study is actually tracking
events.body: The object of study is the in-room evaluation, the weekly office-hours instance, not the attention shift that preceded it and not the twelve-week accumulation that follows it. The shift is treated as origin, the venture-level sheet as destination. Anything the study claims should be read as a claim about this middle process specifically, not about the other two.

events.title: Mentor reactivity cannot be ruled out: they know what I am watching for
events.body: Because the mentors know exactly who you are and what you're there for, you can't rule out that Olivia's and Ravi's judging behavior is shaped by your presence rather than reflecting what they'd do unwatched. You name this as something you have no clean way to check, not something you've found evidence for or against.

events.title: Chloe's memo dates the abandonment before the fifth line
events.body: The memo's "What we have heard" section has several mentors reporting the updates are uniform and that they're reading less into them, and two saying they no longer read them before office hours. That account puts the abandonment before the fifth line arrived in week seven, and the programme's own record is that the line was written to catch what mentors were already doing. So the ordering isn't something you're reconstructing after the fact, it's what the programme itself says happened.

events.title: Strip the fifth line and rescore on the old four
events.body: If you take the command line out and rescore this cohort on the four lines the last cohort also had, and the introduced founders still come out on top, the effect is bigger than the new line and your claim about abandonment holds more broadly. If they don't, and Loomly and Tallow scoring highest on traction is a hint they might not, then the fifth line is carrying the difference, and what you can claim shrinks to a specific chain: the tool emptied the page, the programme wrote the room onto the sheet, and the sheet did the rest. You haven't run this yet, but it's the test that would tell you which version you're in.

events.title: Programme's response to an emptied artefact, not tool bias
events.body: If the rescoring goes the way the researcher expects, the account they're now sitting with is that the required writing tool emptied the artefact of information, and the programme responded by scoring the interaction instead of the writing. The criterion it added to compensate is the one that happens to track prior acquaintance. The researcher is explicit that this puts the causal weight on the programme's response rather than on the tool, and that this is narrower than what they set out expecting, but they think it's truer.

events.title: Discrimination-collapse claim recurs across interview, Slack, and memo
events.body: You can evidence the "instrument stopped discriminating" claim in three separate registers: mentors saying it to you in interview, mentors saying it to each other on Slack, and mentors saying it to Chloe in the memo that changed the scoring sheet. You're flagging this as the part of the mechanism claim you can back most solidly, because it shows up unprompted across three different audiences rather than only in the setting where you asked for it.

events.title: Census at venture level, sample at office-hours and interview level
events.body: The venture is a census, all eighteen ventures' updates, usage logs and Selection Day sheets, so the introduced/open-call split (roughly a third to two thirds) is covered in full at that level. The office-hours slot is a different unit and a sample, about thirty slots across four mentors over ten weeks, and the interview set is smaller still, seven founders picked to fill cells. So whatever the venture-level data can support on its own, the same comparison run through office-hours observation or interviews is resting on much thinner numbers, and I shouldn't let the census cover for the sample when I write this up.

events.title: Mentor confounded with cell for introduced/heavy-use founders
events.body: The founders who are introduced and heavy-use are mostly Ravi's founders in your observed slots, so you can't tell whether what you're seeing is a mentor effect or a route-in/use-intensity effect. Ravi's week-two shift (laptop closed, one word per name) is something you watched directly; Olivia's week-three shift you only have secondhand from her interview; Ethan's account of still reading and not being able to rank fine against fine you only have from Slack. Three different evidence types standing in for what should be the same kind of observation across mentors, and you can't yet separate the mentor from the cell.

events.title: Introduced-plus-light-user cell may be empty in this cohort
events.body: The cell that stays empty either way, introduced founder paired with light tool use, may simply have no occupant this cohort. You're not sure a founder exists who sits in it. If so, any claim your design makes about that cell can't be tested here regardless of how the count comes out, and that's a limit on the comparison, not a finding about it.

events.title: Evaluators judging entrepreneurial potential from a founder's communication will let style cues, not just underlying venture substance, drive their assessment of scalability and long-term growth.
events.body:
Where the expectation holds: The authors say this holds in investor evaluation of founder pitches and tie the mechanism specifically to gender-linked linguistic patterns, not to network access or prior contact.

Where the expectation holds: framed as a general pattern across entrepreneurial resource-mobilization contexts, not specific to accelerator scoring sheets or office-hours formats.

events.title: Introduced founders get longer office-hours slots
events.body: Daniel Kim's slot log shows introduced founders averaging 21 minutes against 13 for open-call founders across weeks 3 to 6 [[chunk:092ca834-03bb-4eea-8682-bc9c84fadd04]], and this shows up live in the fieldnote where Gabriel's slot runs 24 minutes against a scheduled 15 while Hannah and Leah get compressed slots [[chunk:28e11f01-cc47-4ee3-87b2-0596e8a144d2]]. Ethan Brooks names the same pattern about himself: "Gabriel's slot ran 25 mins again. Leah got 11 because I had to leave. Not proud of that" [[chunk:d6d50f0b-9d17-4537-be6e-96abc3e3f3a1]].

events.title: Tool removed writing as a signal, mentors substituted room performance
events.body: Olivia Ward gives the clearest first-person account of the mechanism: the pages became decent for everyone, "the page stopped telling me anything, and I went back to the thing the page was supposed to stop me relying on," which she names as "whether they sound like someone I'd back" [[chunk:533ae601-1f69-4b1b-b9f9-65271b196667]]. Ravi Patel states the same causal chain to Marcus directly: "It made the pages identical, so now all I've got is the room. And the room is not fair, mate, the room is who's comfortable being interrupted" [[chunk:28e11f01-cc47-4ee3-87b2-0596e8a144d2]]. Chloe Park's memo formalizes this substitution by adding a "command of the business" line scored from office-hours contact [[chunk:092ca834-03bb-4eea-8682-bc9c84fadd04]].

events.title: Command score may track rehearsed comfort with interruption rather than command of the venture
events.body: Olivia admits she scored command highest for founders she already had context on "because I knew what they'd been doing before the programme, so I could tell when an answer was real" [[chunk:533ae601-1f69-4b1b-b9f9-65271b196667]]. Gabriel, a former bank product manager, says being interrupted "is how meetings work" and endorses the command line as testing the right thing [[chunk:48c3ba91-ac43-48d1-9089-28fe91d4c87d]], while Hannah Foster, a former teacher, says interruption "reads as not having an answer" for her [[chunk:6da43e6d-6dd5-4b69-ab42-ea802ed3321c]]. This suggests the command score may be measuring rehearsed comfort with a particular conversational style rather than command of the venture itself.

events.title: It's the door, not the deck
events.body: Gabriel offers a competing account of what actually drives the disparity: not the tool's removal of writing as signal, but pre-existing relationships between mentors and introduced founders. Asked whether Hannah would get what he gets if she used the tool identically, he says "No. Not because of the tool. Because Ravi doesn't know anyone she's worked with. It's not the deck, it's the door" [[chunk:da5a5470-8def-41b3-b088-d9ba83098d5e]]. This locates the cause in the introduction network itself rather than in anything the tool changed.

events.title: Hannah Foster keeps two documents each week
events.body: Hannah describes maintaining the required Pitchwright one-pager for the programme alongside a self-made two-column page of "the numbers and what people actually said to me" that she actually uses in the room, because office-hours questions are "never on the page" [[chunk:8daaf22d-d44d-4ed4-b2b8-5fe0d2123984]]. This is directly corroborated in the fieldnote, where Ravi waves away her laptop and looks instead at the page she printed herself [[chunk:f98ca04f-f097-4baf-afa8-c5b90e832ac3]].

events.title: Selection Day grants went entirely to introduced founders
events.body: Daniel Kim's appended note records that all three Selection Day grants (Kerbside, Bramble, Fenwick Labs) went to founders who came in through a mentor introduction, while the two highest-traction open-call ventures, Loomly and Tallow, scored lowest on the new command line [[chunk:f87f37d1-6bf1-4222-8416-cc791b5ef700]]. The note also flags that last cohort, before the tool and before the command line, one of three grants went to an introduced founder, an implicit before/after contrast.

events.title: Ravi runs office hours with the laptop closed
events.body: The fieldnote records Ravi Patel keeping a printed list of eighteen venture names and writing one word next to each after a slot, having stopped reading the Pitchwright updates after week one because "they were the same page with the company name changed" [[chunk:f98ca04f-f097-4baf-afa8-c5b90e832ac3]]. His one-word notes across three consecutive slots ("fine", "solid", "there's something there") are the only visible trace of his scoring process in the field record [[chunk:28e11f01-cc47-4ee3-87b2-0596e8a144d2]].

events.title: Hannah Foster's bind anchors the paper, not a mentor's dilemma
events.body: Olivia, Ravi, and Chloe are all caught between the tool and what it costs, but each of them can name the trade out loud and keeps the job either way, Ravi can say the room isn't fair and carry on running it the next day [[chunk:5424432e-5339-4bc4-89b7-d146dfac7507]]. Hannah names it more precisely than I do, and has no forum at Coldharbour where naming it counts, so she cannot get out of it either: she is required to file the Pitchwright page, Daniel checks that she has, she knows nobody reads it, so she writes a second page by hand for the room, complying and routing around the compliance in the same week [[chunk:8daaf22d-d44d-4ed4-b2b8-5fe0d2123984]]. That's what should anchor the paper, a bind someone is living rather than a dilemma someone with standing is observing.

events.title: Gabriel endorses the very asymmetry that disadvantages him least
events.body: Gabriel states the command-of-business line is "what the programme should be testing, and it's what they are testing now" [[chunk:48c3ba91-ac43-48d1-9089-28fe91d4c87d]], while also acknowledging in the same interview that the tool "cleared the page out of the way so the room is all that's left, which suits me. I'm not going to pretend otherwise" [[chunk:da5a5470-8def-41b3-b088-d9ba83084d5e]]. His endorsement of the fairness of the current arrangement sits alongside his explicit self-interest in it, and the material doesn't resolve whether his account of what the programme "should" test is a genuine belief or a rationalization.

events.title: Leah Morgan's room opened, her command score didn't follow
events.body: The one moment in your week-4 fieldnote where Ravi leans forward for an open-call founder is Leah's, when the question stops being about the page and she tells the kitchen-porter story. He writes "there's something there," warmer than the "fine" he gives Hannah [[chunk:28e11f01-cc47-4ee3-87b2-0596e8a144d2]]. But her command score still came out low, so the room opening didn't carry through to the score the way your account would predict. You're calling this a near miss rather than a counter-case, and I'd leave it exactly that unsettled: it doesn't overturn the pattern, but it isn't absorbed by it either.

events.title: Pattern currently rests on two founders and one aggregate line
events.body: Right now the claim that introduced founders score high on command and open-call founders score low draws on Hannah, Gabriel, and Daniel's note that Loomly and Tallow sit lowest on command and highest on traction [[chunk:f87f37d1-6bf1-4222-8416-cc791b5ef700]]. You haven't read the command line for the other fifteen ventures individually, and you said yourself one of the three grant winners could have scored poorly on command and won on team or market. Until that tabulation is done, the pattern holds at the level of two founders and an aggregate, not a checked census.

events.title: Hannah's diagnosis has no venue that counts as input
events.body: She said it to me in a cafe, off the record. At Coldharbour, the weekly update is the channel, and it's the channel she's describing the problem with. Office hours are fifteen minutes of being interrupted about parent pricing, not a place to make the argument [[chunk:8daaf22d-d44d-4ed4-b2b8-5fe0d2123984]]. The Selection Day sheet has no line for it either, so she can state the trap precisely and still have nowhere at the programme to put the statement, which is why it comes out as a second sheet of paper instead of a complaint [[chunk:6da43e6d-6dd5-4b69-ab42-ea802ed3321c]].

events.title: Hannah's ask is two things the programme can't grant together
events.body: Read the pages, or stop pretending the pages are the point, either one, not both [[chunk:6da43e6d-6dd5-4b69-ab42-ea802ed3321c]]. Granting the second half means conceding, within a single term, that the board paper's stated aim (level the field so mentors judge the venture, not the writing) was wrong. That's the bind underneath her bind, and it's my current best sense of why nothing moves, though I haven't got past naming it that way.

events.title: Chloe's Slack admission becomes the memo's fairness claim
events.body: In week 5, after Daniel posts the slot log, Chloe writes in the mentors' Slack channel that she is proposing the command line "so we are at least scoring the room openly rather than pretending we score the deck" [[chunk:d6d50f0b-9d17-4537-be6e-96abc3e3f3a1]]. That is her naming the contradiction herself, informally, before any memo exists. By the week-7 memo the same move is described as making "explicit what mentors say they are already doing" [[chunk:092ca834-03bb-4eea-8682-bc9c84fadd04]], the same fact with the word "pretending" gone and the board paper's fairness aim left standing, unretracted.

events.title: Board's leveling expectation for the shared writing tool
events.body: The board's January paper commits to a specific claim: mentors couldn't tell whether the venture or the writing was being rated, and a shared writing assistant required of every founder levels this, so mentors will be judging comparable documents for the first time [[chunk:f87f37d1-6bf1-4222-8416-cc791b5ef700]]. You name this as the strongest and most documented expectation held by anyone in the setting, and the one your case breaks. You don't yet say what replaces it, only that this is the expectation whose failure the paper turns on.

This names a comparison without making a claim, and says twice that I have not yet said what the gap means. The collapse it points at is in "Uniform pages stop mentors from reading them" and its three-register evidence in "Discrimination-collapse claim recurs across interview, Slack, and memo", both of which I kept.

The census-against-sample asymmetry is in "Census at venture level, sample at office-hours and interview level" and the specific confound in "Mentor confounded with cell for introduced/heavy-use founders", both kept. Cell counts belong in the sample description, not as a third card.

This is my recall and the card says so. It is not a tally and it calls itself provisional. It can go in once I have counted the slots against the fieldnotes and the usage log; until then it should not sit in the model as a claim.

Cohen, Bingham and Hallen 2019 b is a claim about founders' reasoning quality, and I have no measure of founder cognition at all: I measure slot length, interruption, scores and selection. Its own scope note excludes how a programme's scoring sheet later credits that contact, which is the whole of my case. I kept the paper's other expectation, the one about structured contact building command independent of who introduced the founder.

Clough, Fang, Vissa and Wu 2019 a is Hallen 2008 a restated more loosely, from a review rather than a study, and its scope note ties it to no programme design or instrument. I kept Hallen a for the prior-ties claim and Clough b, which is the sharper thing this review says: that formally open processes still track informal access.

The memo's "makes explicit what mentors are already doing" framing is in "Chloe's Slack admission becomes the memo's fairness claim", which I kept and which has both of her registers side by side. Ravi's contrasting read stays as a quote in the write-up.

The same fifteen minutes as "Leah Morgan's week four slot", re-read through the bind. I kept that card for the episode and "Leah Morgan's room opened, her command score didn't follow" for what it does not settle. Leah as a contrast to Hannah's workaround is a sentence in the write-up, not a third card on one slot.

events.title: Uniform pages stop mentors from reading them contradicts Differences in initial network position persist over time because early access begets further access, so a founder who starts with more contact accumulates a compounding advantage rather than the gap closing on its own.
events.body: You said your setting contradicts this expectation. Show a pattern rather than a single instance: at least two observations from two different documents of your material.

events.title: Uniform pages stop mentors from reading them contradicts Differences in initial network position persist over time because early access begets further access, so a founder who starts with more contact accumulates a compounding advantage rather than the gap closing on its own.
A standing bias, not an emergent compensation
events.body: On this account the programme was already weighting something like prior acquaintance before the tool ever touched the artefact; the emptying didn't cause a new criterion to appear, it just removed the competing signals that had been drowning that old one out. You'd tell this apart from the programme's response to an emptied artefact by rescoring cases where the artefact stayed full, no required tool involved: if the acquaintance-tracking criterion still dominates there, the bias was standing all along, and if it only shows up once the artefact is emptied, that's your account.

day would judge the venture and not the founder's writing. within about three weeks that aim and what the mentors actually did pulled apart. ravi patel stopped reading the updates in week one because they were the same page with the company name changed, and ran office hours with the laptop closed instead: a printed list of eighteen venture names, one word beside each after the slot. his own gloss founders she "already had some context on," the ones introduced through someone.

events.reason: Csaszar, Ketkar and Kim 2024 carries the AI half of this study and was judged to fit, with an expectation, in an earlier pass: founders using the same AI writing tool produce outputs that converge in structure and content. The paper is engaged in my saved Context, Site and Early data answers; what is missing is an expectation the tool will draw.

McMullen and Shepherd 2006 is the conceptual anchor for entrepreneurial action under uncertainty and makes no setting-level prediction by design. It is in the corpus for the theory of judgment under uncertainty the mentors are exercising in the room, not for a testable expectation about a pre-seed programme. Command score tracks founders' theory of what interruption means
events.body: On this account, Gabriel and Hannah aren't at different levels of practice with being cut off, they're running different theories about what a cut-off signals. Gabriel's professional norm codes an interruption as a colleague testing your reasoning, so he answers through it; Hannah's codes it as a verdict that she's already failed, so she folds. For this to beat your comfort-with-interruption explanation, you'd need to see founders who get plenty of exposure to interruption during the programme and still score low because they never stop reading it as a verdict, while someone with little exposure but who's talked through what the interruption is for jumps straight to a high score. That would tell you it's the founder's belief about the interruption doing the work, not how many times they've sat through one, which is different from saying command score may track rehearsed comfort with interruption rather than command of the venture.

The paper is about the tool's design, not any one person's bind
events.body: What anchors this isn't a person at all, it's Pitchwright itself: a system built to be filed and not read, which produces the same compliance-plus-workaround pattern in anyone who has to touch it, Hannah included. For this to be the better account, you'd need to see the doubling (file the form, then do the real work by hand) show up wherever the tool sits in the workflow, regardless of who's assigned to it and whether they can name the bind or not; if Hannah's replacement did the same two-page dance in her first month, that's the tool talking, not her particular clarity about her situation. That would compete directly with "Hannah Foster's bind anchors the paper, not a mentor's dilemma," which needs the anchor to be her specific, articulate, standing-less position, not a structural feature that would catch anyone in that seat.

events.text: Yes, one: Leah Morgan. Open call, first venture, and Ravi had no outside context on her at all. She delivered the Pitchwright deck as a monologue, he told her to forget all of it and asked what the restaurant actually said, she froze, and then told him about the kitchen porter being the person who decides. He leaned forward for the first time in that slot and wrote "there's something there". Hannah Foster, also open call, got "fine". So the room did reward being pushed, once, without acquaintance. What did not follow is her command score: Leah and Loomly scored highest on traction and lowest on command on the Selection Day sheet. While I am here, the passage your check says nothing cites is my own note at the foot of that fieldnote: count interruptions per slot next week, check who came in through an introduction, the open-call founders are getting the shorter slots. That matters because it dates my noticing of the slot-length gap to week 4, in the room, three weeks before I had Daniel Kim's log to put numbers on it. The interruption count it promises I never did.

events.title: Leah Morgan's belief about who actually decides
events.body: Leah is the one person in the study who states something about what makes a venture worth funding that isn't reducible to how the scoring process will register it: the fat-collection business turns on the kitchen porter, not the manager, being the one who decides. That's a claim about how the restaurant actually works, not a guess about what Ravi wants to hear. It surfaced only once he told her to drop the deck and ask what happened, and it's what made him lean in and write "there's something there" [[chunk:28e11f01-cc47-4ee3-87b2-0596e8a144d2]].

events.question: What made you stop counting interruptions after week 4, and is there any record of why you dropped that thread?
events.reason: You've told me the interruption count was promised and never done, and I want to know whether that gap is just fieldwork attrition or whether something in the material made you decide it wasn't the right measure.

events.text:
That note to self is a good find, it dates your noticing to week 4 and it also tells me something about how you were watching at the time: you'd already grouped Gabriel with Samuel and Natalie as introduced, and you were already predicting shorter slots for open-call founders, three weeks before you had Daniel's numbers to confirm it. That's early data doing its job, showing you something before you had the apparatus to measure it. But the promise in that same note, count interruptions per slot, is the one you flagged as never completed, and it's sitting right next to a fieldnote where you did count them for one slot, Hannah's, four in eleven minutes. So you have at least one number and a plan to get more that you dropped.

What made you stop counting interruptions after week 4, and is there anything, a memo, a Slack message, a later fieldnote, that tells you why?

First a correction to what I just typed: Tallow is Leah's venture, Loomly is Hannah's. The two open-call ventures that scored highest on traction and lowest on command are Loomly and Tallow. On the interruptions: I have three counts from that one afternoon, not one. Hannah four in eleven minutes, Gabriel once in twenty-four, Leah none until Ravi stopped her outright. I dropped it because I could not settle what counts as an interruption, a number question, a redirection, or an interjection that takes the floor, and without a written definition I did not trust my own tallies across four mentors. There is no record of the decision. It fell off between weeks four and five while I was chasing the sheet change instead. It is recoverable: the fieldnotes name the founder and the start time for every slot, so recoding ten weeks against one written definition is work I can do from material I already hold, without going back to anyone.

events.question: What would your working definition of "interruption" be if you wrote it down today, and would it count Ravi's opening redirects the same way as his mid-answer cutoffs?
events.reason: You can't recode the ten weeks of fieldnotes you already hold until you've fixed the category, and the shape of that definition will decide whether Gabriel's one interruption in twenty-four minutes and Hannah's four in eleven are even comparable numbers.

events.text:
That's a clean account of a methodological loss, three counts on one afternoon, no written definition, then the thread dropped while you chased the sheet change. It's recoverable, and the fact that you can name exactly when and why it stopped is itself useful. But I want to press on something you said almost in passing: you don't trust your own tallies across four mentors without a written definition. That's the real obstacle to recoding, not the absence of data.

What would you count as an interruption if you sat down today to write that definition, and would it treat Ravi's redirect to Hannah, "tell me what happened this week," the same way it treats him cutting off Leah's monologue?

No, and that is the distinction I never drew. An interruption, if I write it down today, is a mentor turn that takes the floor before the founder has finished the unit they were delivering, counted once per turn regardless of length. On that definition Ravi's four number questions to Hannah are four, and his one interjection to Gabriel is one. Ravi's opening redirect is a different act entirely. Waving away Hannah's laptop, or telling Leah to forget the deck, does not interrupt her speech, it refuses the artefact before she has used it. That is the behaviour the whole study is about, so it should be its own count, not folded into interruptions. So two tallies per slot: artefact refusals at the opening, and floor-taking during the answer. I would rather have two small honest counts than one number that hides the difference between a mentor who will not read the page and a mentor who talks over you.

events.title: Interruption redefined as floor-taking, separate from artefact refusal
events.body: Working definition as of today: an interruption is a mentor turn that takes the floor before the founder finishes the unit they were delivering, counted once per turn regardless of length. On this definition Ravi's four number questions to Hannah are four interruptions and his one interjection to Gabriel is one, but waving away Hannah's laptop or telling Leah to forget the deck doesn't count as an interruption at all, it refuses the artefact before she's used it [[chunk:8daaf22d-d44d-4ed4-b2b8-5fe0d2123984]] [[chunk:28e11f01-cc47-4ee3-87b2-0596e8a144d2]]. Because the artefact refusal is the behavior the whole study is about, it gets its own tally rather than folding into the interruption count. Two counts per slot going forward: artefact refusals at the opening, floor-taking during the answer, kept separate so the difference between a mentor who won't read the page and a mentor who talks over you doesn't get hidden inside one number.

events.text:
Splitting artefact refusal from floor-taking is going to matter later when you're coding Ravi against Olivia against Ethan, since your fieldnote already shows Ravi refusing the artefact at the door (waving away Hannah's laptop, telling Leah to forget the deck) in a way I haven't seen you document for the other two mentors at all. But right now I want to stay on early data, not on the coding scheme.

You've given me four things you didn't expect, and each one came from watching the process you set out to track: mentors stopping, the sheet change, the traction/command split, Gabriel's self-aware defense. What I haven't heard is anything that surprised you from a source you weren't already treating as evidence for this study, something you read or heard almost by accident, before you knew it belonged in the puzzle at all.

events.subject: early-data
events.statement:
Four things the material has shown me that I did not go in expecting.

Mentors stopped reading the page rather than reading it differently. I expected polished, comparable updates to be judged more alike. Instead Olivia Ward stopped at about week three because everybody's pages were decent and that was the problem, Ravi Patel stopped in week two after three updates that were the same page with the company name changed, and Ethan Brooks kept reading and found he could not rank fine against fine. A tool brought in to make the artefact comparable made it uninformative.

The programme then wrote the room onto the sheet. Chloe Park's week-7 memo adds "Founder command of the business", scored from office-hours contact rather than the deck, and says in terms that this makes explicit what mentors are already doing. Within seven weeks the organisation formalised the thing the intervention was meant to remove, in writing, and said so.

The founders with the best evidence were the ones the new criterion punished. Loomly and Tallow scored highest on traction and lowest on command. I had assumed command and substance would at least point the same way.

The advantaged founder is not unaware of his advantage. I expected Gabriel Martinez to tell a merit story. He does not: he says the page was never the field, that the tool has cleared the page out of the way so the room is all that is left, which suits him, and that it is not the deck, it is the door. He also thinks the room is the right test. That is a competing theory of what should count as evidence, held by the person it favours, and it is not obviously wrong.

What cuts against the pattern, and what I have not checked. The one moment the room opened for an open-call founder is Leah Morgan's week-4 slot: she delivered the Pitchwright deck as a monologue, Ravi told her to forget it and asked what the restaurant actually said, and she gave him the kitchen porter. That is the only point in that fieldnote where he leans forward, and he wrote "there's something there" rather than the "fine" Hannah got. Her command score still came out low. On the other side I have not read the command line for the fifteen ventures I did not interview, so I cannot yet rule out an introduced founder scoring badly on command, or an open-call founder scoring well simply because they are comfortable being interrupted. Gabriel's account predicts the latter should exist. Until I tabulate all eighteen I am arguing from two founders and an aggregate, and I will say so rather than round it up.

One more thing the material shows that I had stopped seeing. The last paragraph of my own week-4 fieldnote is a note to self: count interruptions per slot next week, check who came in through an introduction, the open-call founders are getting the shorter slots. That dates my noticing of the slot-length gap to week 4, in the room, three weeks before Daniel Kim's log gave me 21 minutes against 13 to put under it. It also records a measurement I promised myself and never made. I have three counts from that one afternoon and no more: Hannah four interruptions in eleven minutes, Gabriel one in twenty-four, Leah none until Ravi stopped her outright. I dropped the tally because I could not settle what counts, and I will not pretend otherwise. Recoding is possible from material I already hold, and it needs two counts per slot rather than one: artefact refusals at the opening, where a mentor puts the page aside before the founder has used it, and floor-taking during the answer. Those are different acts, and only the first is the behaviour this study is about.

baselines.expectation: New organizations founded with stronger initial network ties secure more favorable early resource access and evaluative treatment than those founded without such ties, independent of the underlying quality of the venture.
baselines.scope: Holds for new organizations at or near founding, drawing on network-position data from the founding period rather than later stages of firm development.

events.subject: sample
events.statement:
The sample has to vary on three things for the comparisons to hold: route into the programme (introduced through a mentor against the open call), prior business vocabulary (corporate, MBA or family business against a first venture), and Pitchwright use (heavy against light, from the usage log). The previous cohort supplies the fourth line of variation, the same sheet without the tool.

There are two units. The venture is the unit for anything countable, and there the variation is already present because it is a census rather than a sample: all eighteen ventures' weekly updates, their usage figures, and their Selection Day sheets, plus the previous cohort's sheets on the four shared lines. Roughly a third of the eighteen came in introduced, two thirds through the open call. The office-hours slot is the second unit and the one where the judgment is actually formed, and that is a sample: about thirty slots across four mentors over ten weeks. Seven founder interviews were chosen to fill cells, Hannah Foster and Leah Morgan open call, Gabriel Martinez, Samuel Price and Natalie Hayes introduced, crossed with heavy and light use.

Three weaknesses I have to state rather than manage. First, the slot sample is mentor-weighted: Ravi Patel's Thursday office hours carries close to half of it, so the attention shift I can document as observation is his. Olivia Ward's I have from her week-six interview and Ethan Brooks's only from the Slack channel. In the observed slots the introduced and heavy-use founders are mostly Ravi's founders, so mentor and cell are not separable yet. Second, Olivia's slots skew open-call and Ethan's are the short ones, so simply watching them more adds coverage without rebalancing the cells. Third, introduced plus light user may not exist as a lived combination in this cohort, which would mean route in and usage are confounded in who the founders are, not merely in who I watched, and neither comparison could then stand alone.

Two things I can settle without new fieldwork, and will before I write this section: cross-tabulate the observed slots by mentor, route in and usage from the fieldnotes, which name the founder and start time for every slot, and check the usage log for whether the introduced/light cell exists across all eighteen. Crossed both ways at interview level the cells stay one or two deep, and I will report them that way.

What has to be run before this goes to a journal, not planned. The check is right that an AMJ reviewer will not accept a causal story about the programme's response resting on two interviewed founders and one aggregate contrast. Three things move from intention to completed work before submission, and all three run on material already in my drive. First, tabulate the command line and the four shared lines for all eighteen ventures in this cohort, so the traction-against-command inversion is a distribution rather than Loomly and Tallow. Second, run the rescore on the old four lines and report it against the pre-registered expectation I wrote at Outcome, which is that the introduced founders would not still be on top. Third, recode the ten weeks of fieldnotes for artefact refusals and floor-taking per slot against a written definition, which turns the stopping-rate claim from something I noticed into something I measured. Until the third is done the stopping rate stays labelled as noticed and not measured, and the claim it supports is stated as two mentors' timing and reasons corroborated across interview, Slack and memo, not as a cohort-level rate.

events.text: You expected Pitchwright to level the field so Selection Day would judge the venture and not the founder's writing, "so that Selection Day would judge the venture and not the founder's writing." Instead you found the programme wrote a new criterion onto the sheet, "Founder command of the business," scored from office-hours contact, and Olivia Ward gave her highest command scores to founders she already had context on, the ones introduced through someone, while Daniel Kim's log gives open-call founders 13 minutes against 21 for introduced.
